utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour -- Your Honours, thank you very much. I would first of all like to apologise to the interpreters for what happened yesterday. They were barely able to interpret --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. My colleagues have pointed this out to me. Are there any other parties in the hearing other than those who were here yesterday? I don't think so. utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would simply for the record note that the Prosecution's case manager for today is Ms. Lourdes Galicia, who is a different case manager to who we had yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. That's fine. I'm very glad and I would like to thank my colleagues for pointing this out to me, but I apologise to your colleague for not having noticed her immediately. I hope she will forgive me even if -- when we resume we usually don't have the appearances. So we will resume. We can now start, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there haven't been any changes in the very large Defence team, so there is no need for us to introduce ourselves. I really wanted to apologise to the interpreters for what happened yesterday. It was difficult for them to interpret everything that I said. Today I will try and satisfy all three conditions; I will try and state what I consider to be essential without repeating myself, and I will try to do this in a reasonable period of time so that it can be correctly interpreted. So the first ground of appeal of the Defence is a matter of fact which is of great importance. It concerns the position of Krnojelac, of the accused, the de jure and de facto position in the KPD during the relevant period. When we made this ground of appeal, we did it because we considered that the numerous evidence and the numerous facts that has been presented and their fairly large significance represented a dramatic basis, and on this basis one could claim that not a single reasonable Trial Chamber would be able to reach the conclusion that the accused Krnojelac did have the position as described by the Prosecution -- by the Trial Chamber. Perhaps the Defence in its brief failed to mention this, and that is perhaps due to certain terminological characteristics of the translation. The word "reasonable" which in the mother tongue of the Defence means something that is not rational. So that can also be an offensive term. That is why in our brief we decided to use the term "the errors made by the Trial Chamber," but in our opinion those errors are such that if one uses the language that has been accepted, that has been established in this Tribunal, it is our opinion that the facts had an influence on the Trial Chamber and made them reach a determination on the basis of an erroneous interpretation of facts. So when we say that the Trial Chamber, with regard to this essential basis for determining criminal responsibility, this essential factual basis for determining the accused's responsibility, of course we believe that it is of crucial significance for all the other counts on which the accused has been declared guilty, given that the essence of the discussion with regard to this count is formally and factually concerns the position of the accused. And this position has to be established if we are to be able to establish his criminal responsibility with regard to the counts in the indictment on the basis of which he has been declared guilty. The Defence in this first ground of appeal -- the Defence has divided this first ground of appeal into several subgrounds, and I will try to resume this in a very concise way and present arguments for each subground. First of all, we believe that the Trial Chamber concluded erroneously with regard to the unchanged structure in the KPD after the conflict had broken out. And also, it made a mistake with regard to the authority of the warden within the KPD. We believe that, given all the circumstances that the Trial Chamber has dealt with, given all the circumstances of the specific period and the specific location in question, the Defence believes that it would be logical to conclude that the authorities and the functioning of the KPD in peacetime, before the conflict broke out, could not continue after the conflict broke out. In other words, there must have been a change. We believe that the Trial Chamber made a mistake when it decided that it wasn't convinced that the authority of the warden within the KPD had changed in a significant manner after the conflict broke out. And in our written submissions, we have also tried to present all this evidence, all this voluminous evidence, which directly shows this and enables us to establish that the Trial Chamber did not reach a reasonable conclusion when they decided that the authority of the warden did not change, that the authority the warden had was the same. So the arguments of the Trial Chamber that the accused, by the Ministry of Justice on the 17th of June, 1992, was appointed as warden without any restrictions, this conclusion is erroneous and has been considered from a one-sided point of view. The Trial Chamber considered that the accused was appointed by the Ministry of Justice as warden. That is not in dispute. But when he was appointed, and that consisted of just one sentence, there is no specific description of his authorities. And for this reason, the Defence presented other evidence which directly and indirectly determines the scope of his authority and the scope of his duties, the scope of the accused's authority and duties. So there is evidence that the accused was appointed as the KPD warden by the Ministry of Justice. He wasn't appointed by the military authorities. He wasn't appointed by the police authorities. He was appointed by the Ministry of Justice of Republika Srpska. When we relate this information to what the Trial Chamber found and established in this decision on appointment, the scope of his duties and authority has not been specified. As support for this, the Defence refers to the exhibit of the Prosecution, P2, and Defence Exhibit D85. And I have to admit -- just allow me to digress for a minute. This would also be a response to the question put by Judge Guney yesterday with regard to the positive authority that the accused had, and I think it is my right to explain something with regard to this question and Judge Schomburg's question, to explain something to which the Prosecution provided an explanation in its brief. If we are talking about the document P2 that was obtained by the Prosecution, it quite clearly and unambiguously states -- and that's a report which the warden who came after Milorad Krnojelac forwarded to the Ministry of Justice for the needs of this Tribunal, and there he states that part of the KPD, and he mentions the number of the decision, the date of the decision, part of the KPD that was -- were used earlier on - and they used this term "earlier on," so that means the continuity has been interrupted - the purpose of it was for the detention of those who had been convicted. That included the kitchen and the hospital. And it had been handed over to the commander of the Tactical Group Foca, to the military authorities. What is also important, and this is something stated further on in the text, it states that on the basis of that contract, that agreement, the commander of the Foca Tactical Group designated those who would be responsible for certain duties and tasks. And they had nothing to do with the civilians. They were not related to the civilians who were engaged in work in the KPD. So this document quite clearly shows that there was a sort of duality within the KPD, a sort of division. It says very clearly in this document that it was leased to the military authorities and that the military authorities designated people who would be responsible for certain tasks. And later on, we will rely on other documents to show that this concerns the guards too who were guarding convicted people. And those people appointed by the military authorities were not connected to the civilians who worked in the KPD. So this report shows that in addition to the military personnel, those appointed by the military authorities, there was civilians and there was no connection between the two. In our belief, this proof is sufficient to show that there was a sort of duality as far as the functioning of KPD is concerned. And the accused mentioned this in his interview before the beginning of the trial, and there is other evidence that supports the claim that this was the reality on the ground. So in order to legally support such a finding, such a position on the part of the Defence, it's important, and I would like to add that this is also a response to a question put yesterday, the question as to how D85 exhibit should be valued, this exhibit, Defence Exhibit D85, is a report of the ward -- of the warden to the Ministry of Justice. It's a report about personnel, about the duties that they had, and it is quite possible to reach a certain conclusion as to the scope of the accused's duties, as to the positive authority that the accused had. If this report is analysed, then it is peculiar from the contents of the document that the warden, and the accused signed the report, makes a distinction between the KPD workers who were, first of all, in the report, and this was supported by many witnesses of the Prosecution. It was clearly established that about 27 persons both of Serbian and Muslim nationality were still staying in the KPD, and they were serving their sentences there, but they didn't take advantage of the opportunity to leave the KPD when the conflict broke out. So there were 27 persons who were serving a sentence, serving their sentences, and that was the reason for which the institution had been established. Even before the conflict, it functioned as a KPD in which there were convicted persons serving their sentences. There was still people there who were under the Ministry of Justice. The accused in his interview and other evidence too shows that he was responsible for those persons. The persons were the responsibility of the Ministry of Justice. And the report that the Defence is referring to shows that the accused was responsible because he only mentioned and reported facts about these people, because the other detainees of Muslim nationality were the responsibility of the military authorities. And there is other evidence to support this claim. I will turn to that evidence later on. I won't concentrate on it for a long period of time given the time restrictions, but it has is all been mentioned in the Defence's brief. In addition to this report to the Ministry of Justice which shows who the accused Krnojelac was responsible for, in this document it can also be seen what his other responsibilities were, and that relates to taking care of the KPD property, because the KPD was the property of the Ministry of Justice. The second part of the accused's authority, and that involved taking care of those who were serving their sentences. And we will see in -- this also concerned a semi-open system of serving a sentence. His duties also included guarding, taking care of the property that was the property of the Ministry of Justice whose employee he was. In the course of the proceedings, it has also been shown that even before the conflict broke out in the Foca territory, the KPD had an economic unit, the name of which was Drina. This was a significant economic factor in peacetime in that area. Now, we've also seen, on the basis of voluminous evidence that the Defence relies on that one of the task of the accused involved taking care of this property, repairing the damage caused by the shelling of the KPD, and also by animating the Drina Economic Unit which was in fact the only economic unit in wartime conditions which was in a position to feed, to a certain extent at least, the detainees and the people, the inhabitants of the town of Foca. When we analyse this report, it is clear from the report that these detainees, that is to say the people, the persons who were serving their sentence, who were mostly involved in the farm of the KPD which was about six kilometres away from the KPD, and they were in a semi-open -- they had a semi-open system of accommodation, and the accused was also responsible for that farm as an employee of the Ministry of Justice. In the report, it is clear that there were six problematic cases within the grounds of the KPD, people who had earlier on been convicted for alcoholism, for drug abuse, and for those reasons, they were not able to be on the farm. Is it possible in wartime conditions when there is a lack of essentials, would it be possible for the accused to organise a special sector or special security for six individuals who were serving their sentence in semi-open conditions? It's quite clear that those six individuals should be detained in the part that is under the command of the military authorities and that they shouldn't have a special security system or special kitchen organised for them. As it states in the report, they were placed in that part because of alcoholism, because of drug abuse, and so on. So with all due respect, this has caused confusion among the Prosecution, and this is why they have stated that there was unified guard system. The Defence thinks that there is a lot of evidence and a lot of testimony that shows that these workers were workers who were sent by the army to the KPD, and the first -- the Trial Chamber's -- the first instance judgement shows that these people spent part of their time standing guard and part of their time -- and another part of the time was spent by going to the front. So they had divided duties. This will be something to support the Defence's claim that the accused was not the superior of these people who were not employed by the Ministry of Justice. They didn't fall under the responsibility, under the command of the accused. They didn't come under his responsibility. The Defence provided other evidence that supports this claim. The letter from the Executive Committee in which they required material for repairs to the roof, for locating vehicles for the KPD, this evidence shows the scope of the accused's duties. It shows what he was involved with in the course of his work, which was from 7.00 to 3.00 p.m. Those are the usual working hours for such a person but not the usual working hours for the commander of a camp in which there were Muslim detainees. By itself, this shows that such a claim, such a position on the part of the Trial Chamber cannot be supported. The Defence also included in its exhibits a number of travel orders in which it states - and they were signed by Krnojelac - it says the warden, the director of the economic unit. And these travel orders -- these travel orders also included a description of the duties, of the work carried out by the accused and the reason for which so many trips were made by the accused. And doesn't this show, together with all this other evidence, what the responsibilities of the accused were? So if we compare this to the findings of the Trial Chamber according to which there were no changes to the structure in the KPD and that therefore he was in a position of authority and in a position of responsibility, it is our belief that some other reasonable Trial Chamber would not be able to reach such a conclusion on this basis. These travel orders that the Defence has included in its exhibits come from various periods during his -- during the time Milorad Krnojelac spent in the KPD. In addition to what the Defence claims, we would also like to refer to Exhibit -- the Prosecution Exhibit P3, which included a list of people who had work and obligations to carry out in the KPD. And this list shows - and Prosecution witnesses of Muslim nationality have also mentioned this, Muslim individuals who worked in the KPD earlier on - this shows that until the conflict broke out, the KPD had a warden, had a manager of the economic unit Drina, Milenko Simovic, and Exhibit P3 shows that from August 1993, Radojica Tesovic, who was in May -- who was in the KPD from May, became the director of the Drina Economic Unit. So it is clear according to this list and all the other evidence that during this period from the time when the conflict broke out up until the time that Milorad Krnojelac left the KPD, there was no economic unit. With all this evidence, with all these travel orders, with all the indications in travel orders of his post, manager of the Drina Economic Unit, manager of the enterprise and so on and so forth, shows once again that during the relevant period indicated in the indictment, that is what Milorad Krnojelac was responsible for. I am talking about all this because I think it is absolutely -- should be accorded preference for all the other counts of indictment in terms of chains of command and possible other omissions which could see -- which speak of a significant support and aid to perpetrators of crimes, because the time, the hours that the accused spends in the penitentiary are of major importance with regard to what the Prosecution spoke about, alarming information, and his liability under counts which the Defence challenges. Therefore, for all these reasons, and if we look at it from the point of view of a war conflict in a small and poor locality, it is quite clear that the structure in the penitentiary did not go on unchanged, nor -- or that Milorad Krnojelac at -- in wartime had the same powers as the warden will have in peacetime. We also think that the Chamber erroneously concluded that he accepted the duty of a warden of his own free will. We addressed the nature of his duties and the jobs he carried out, and we, however, also think that the Trial Chamber made a mistake in this instance too. The Trial Chamber, when making this conclusion, speaks of two grounds which make it arrive at that particular conclusion. The first is that there are two persons who refused the job and suffered no consequences whatsoever. They are Radojica Tesovic and Veselin Cancar. When speaking about these two persons, we believe that the Trial Chamber should not rely on this type of evidence. First, from the Prosecution's Exhibit P3, we clearly see that from -- that Radojica Tesovic is in the penitentiary as of May 1993 when the warden has already been appointed, and the Prosecution's witness testimony shows that Radojica Tesovic left Foca for Crna Gora with a certain number of persons of Muslim ethnicity. So at the time when people are being assigned to labour obligations, we clearly see that at least one person, Radojica Tesovic, is not in Foca any more. As for the other person, Veselin Cancar, the Trial Chamber draws the conclusion that he refused the job from the statement that he gave to the cantonal court in Sarajevo. The Defence challenges that statement during the proceedings. The Prosecution intended to call that witness for cross-examination as to that fact, however, he refused to do that and so that person was not called here to testify and be cross-examined. The Defence tried since the Criminal Proceedings Act changed, but the new law on Bosnia-Herzegovina took over the SFRY legislation. We tried to see that under that law, the accused had the right to defend himself before the Court and -- because he is not a witness who was sworn in this case and therefore was not bound to speak the truth. The Defence, we admit, did not present a set of Bosnian laws which would be applicable in this case, but nevertheless, we thought we should draw the attention of this Appeals Chamber to this because we are talking about one's act of free will or not as the question which arose is whether on the 16th of April, 1992, the accused Milorad Krnojelac knew that Radojica Tesovic was there, or Veselin Cancar. Did he know that those two individuals refused the offer and suffered no consequences for it? Because it is only on that basis that we can determine or perhaps draw a parallel between an act of his own free will and the acts of free will of those two -- those two other individuals, because the condition that has to be established is that at the time when he was assigned to this labour obligation, that at that time he knew of what we have just spoken about. And finally, if we accept the principle that is propounded by the constitution as to one's free will, then we can also resolve to the same kind of argument. The Defence, therefore, refers to Exhibit -- to an exhibit it produced to show that the labour obligation was practically a combat assignment, a wartime assignment under the conditions of an armed conflict. The labour assignment, and I believe this holds true over the majority of countries, is something that is mandatory, something that is compulsory, something which if not obeyed, if not complied with, may lead to imprisonment or detention. The Defence has produced evidence to this effect showing that it was a labour obligation which practically meant -- which was tantamount to a wartime assignment under the conditions of an armed conflict. Likewise, to draw a parallel, that is, this act of free will stand corroborated by the fact that in 1993, the accused requested to go back to his teaching job. And from the point of view of the Defence deems it untenable because one cannot draw a parallel between that particular moment when the armed conflict broke out, when fighting broke out and when you are therefore under a labour obligation as your wartime assignment, and 1993, that is 15 months later, because the circumstances changed. They were bound to. And therefore, it also had to affect the state of mind and one's thinking whether now one could perhaps look for another job without any adverse consequences. And evidently, the accused deemed that that was the case, and he asked to be allowed to go back to his old job, that is, the instruction of mathematics. He's been a maths teacher all his life. And therefore, he is a person of an age of which he is, and at that time, perhaps he was seen as a person who could manage an economic enterprise, an economic unit. So, as far as I'm concerned with regard to this subground of appeal (C) we think the Trial Chamber erred with regard to the chain of command or the hierarchy which reigned in the KP Dom. It has been established beyond a doubt and the first instance judgement also speaks of a contract, a contract whereby the KP Dom was leased. Perhaps that document does not look like an international contract, but it is beyond any doubt a contract between two parties. Were Milorad Krnojelac, anywhere in the chain of command of the military authority, well, in that case he wouldn't have been concluding a contract with a superior commander. He would have been simply issued an order to put a particular part of the KP Dom in the proper service. A contract always means that there are two parties. There are two counterparts. It does not presume a chain of command. And I believe that this is self-explanatory. Alongside all the other evidence showing that the authority or the detained Muslims arrested with the army. When one reads carefully this agreement which is not long, one sees that the military authority is duty-bound to use those facilities, to look after them, and to then return them in -- as they were before after the use. Also, the exhibit of the Prosecution, P2, speaks about the buildings where the detained persons are kept, the kitchen and the infirmary. And this is also important when it comes to determining the responsibility of the accused. To corroborate this conclusion at which the Defence has arrived, we also produced our Exhibit D39, which is applicable to this. This is a report on the prisons within the ministry -- under the Ministry of Justice of the Republika Srpska which says that the district prison in Doboj is faced with an identical situation because the report of the person from the Ministry of Justice, it says that the district prison in Doboj has been ceded to the army for the accommodation of prisoners of war with the clear reference that the security in that prison is in the hands of the army. So amongst the exhibits we have the report of the Ministry of Justice which refers to the northern part of Bosnia, that his presence in the northern part of Bosnia and where we see that Doboj is yet another establishment where the same principle is applied, that is that part of that penitentiary is leased to the army and the army undertakes to provide the security, that is, guards and all the rest goes with it. Now, in view of the time we have at our disposal and in view of the importance of that particular fact, I'd like to address the statement of a witness for the Prosecution which shows unambiguously that in addition to this formal de jure relationship which we tried to show and which also shows the factual authority, that is, who had the factual authority in the penitentiary. A witness for the Prosecution, FWS-86, in his testimony before the Court, says that the factual authority over the prisoners of war was in the hand of a military group which before that, as part of the Uzice Battalion and subsequently the Livade Company within -- of the technical group of Foca. So the Witness 86 says that in the early days of the conflict when that witness was brought to the KP Dom from Milorad Krnojelac who happened to be there, he asked him to leave the KP Dom for a -- for a while. And the gist of the answer of the witness shows that Milorad Krnojelac was not the one who could decide that, that he had to ask the military commander who was responsible for that and to ask him. And the condition was that Milorad Krnojelac's son should go with that person in order to ensure that he would come back. So this witness also shows who had the factual power. Because if we agree that in peacetime the warden has no authority to either lock people up or let then go, but he does have the authority to allow a prisoner to go somewhere outside the prison. To corroborate this argument, we have another testimony of another witness for the Prosecution, and that is the manager of the Maglic Company, Dzevad Lojo who very clearly and unambiguously said that he had asked, because he had known the accused before the war, that he had asked for a meeting with him. A soldier took him to him, and then the soldier -- during that conversation, a soldier wearing a camouflage uniform entered the office during the conversation, interrupted -- kept interrupting them to make it clear to them that that conversation was not particularly allowed and it had to be ended. Now, my question is which warden, with all the prerogatives of power in peacetime conditions can hypothesise such a situation, that a soldier in military uniform enters the warden's office, butts into the conversation, says that such a conversation is not allowed and makes him interrupt that conversation? If we know what the prerogatives of a warden are, if we know what a warden is, perhaps he's not the person who can detain and set free persons, but surely he is at liberty to talk with persons who are in detention at his prison. Can you imagine a situation where -- when a guard tells the warden that he is not allowed to talk to a detainee and that this conversation is to be cut short? I think that this clearly shows the factual authority or, rather, the absence of the factual authority of Milorad Krnojelac. I think this evidence is quite sufficient to show that he did not have that factual authority. So insofar as the chain of command is concerned, the Trial Chamber erred when it concluded that the chief of guards, Mitar Rasevic and deputy warden Savo Todovic, that they were still accountable to the warden and that the warden still had the powers which he used now and then to launch disciplinary measures against his subordinates who did not treat detainees properly. The Defence wishes to draw the attention to the already mentioned Prosecution's Exhibit P3, and perhaps it was due to a mistake of the Trial Chamber that it was not concluded that Savo Todovic became an assistant deputy of the warden for legal and financial matters in August 1993, that is, this exhibit clearly shows that be it as a deputy or be it as an assistant, but he nevertheless begins to work there in August 1993, even though he is there as of May 1993. The report which was produced by the Prosecution, we see that nobody knows what his position is until August 1993. One assumes that he was in the penitentiary, but he was appointed deputy warden only as late as August when Milorad Krnojelac left the KP Dom. So when we look at this exhibit with all the information, all the data concerning persons who work in the KP Dom and when we juxtapose it with the testimony of a witness who was heard before this Tribunal, Witness Dolas, who explicitly, directly talks about his experience, about his firsthand knowledge about what he saw with his own eyes when he worked in the headquarters of the Hercegovina Corps. So this firsthand eyewitness says that Savo Todovic himself told him on one occasion that he was the commander, that he was the -- that he was Muslim prisoners' commander, the commander of those Muslim detainees who were in the KP Dom. This witness, Radomir Dolas, says how when he worked in the personnel department of the command of the Foca Brigade how he had found a document there and seen a document there clearly showing that General Paprica, the brigade commander, had sent --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. I wish to remind you that we are not reopening the hearing here. We are not reopening the debate. You should not speak about things that were already discussed before the Chamber. What you have to do is draw certain conclusions. It is perhaps sometimes difficult to draw -- to make the distinction. The Chamber, however, reminded you yesterday about the conditions and what does it mean to work in -- before a Chamber of Appeals, which is not the same as a Trial Chamber. So will you please remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. My apologies. I will try. I merely wished to acquaint the Appeals Chamber with the facts by referring to exhibits. But I will try to avoid that in the future. So there is ample evidence which in one way or another points in that direction, and we have already indicated them in our appeal brief. There is ample evidence showing that the accused had no factual authority, not even, we think, the de jure authority, that he was in no way responsible for persons who were kept in that part of the KP Dom or that he had any authority over the prison guards. The Defence also reminds, and of course I'm not going to analyse it in view of what His Honour the President has just said, but the Defence has also produced numerous exhibits showing lists of exchanges, lists for exchange signed by Marko Kovac, showing who will be released, who will be exchanged. There are other orders signed by the commander of the Tactical Group. We also produced evidence to show that this self-same commander of that Tactical Group issued the permits to visit somebody in detention. That is, there is simply no evidence to show the factual authority, the factual authority of the accused Milorad Krnojelac over the persons of Muslim origin. There is absolutely no exhibits to show that he had any effective control or any effective power to do anything in that regard. When we speak about the factual and formal powers of Milorad Krnojelac in the KP Dom, then I think it is necessary, and I'm saying -- I'm not going to go back to that. I merely comment on what we've already extensively shown in our brief, and that is that numerous witnesses of Muslim origin who were detained in the KP Dom and who were called by the Prosecution, they were indirect witnesses. They had the first hand experience. And we heard them use expressions because they tell us about their impressions. And so they say Milorad Krnojelac was just a paper commander, or Milorad Krnojelac was de facto warden. Power over us, the authority over us, was in the hands of Savo Todovic, was in the hands of the military command. No, I'm sorry. I said de facto and I said de jure, that he was the commander merely de jure but that the actual authority over them had the military command, and the military command was responsible for them. So the Defence does not dispute that the accused Milorad Krnojelac had the title of a warden, but I think it did not suffice to allow the Prosecution to establish his factual control or authority over the prisoners of Muslim -- of Muslim ethnicity or over persons who are charged with war crimes as direct perpetrators of crimes. When we talk about persons who are charged as direct perpetrators and who are charged under 7(3) of the -- and -- and for which Milorad Krnojelac is accused under 7(3) as their superior, we do not think that -- we think it is untenable, because any reasonable Tribunal of fact must have been clear that such hierarchy was absent, such chain of command was absent. They must have remembered that those persons, and we have documents to show it, that they were persons who were assigned to particular jobs by the military, and it was the military, the army responsible for those persons. I'm referring to all those who were on guard duty. And of course I'm not going to go back to all the exhibits that we indicated in our brief. Therefore -- so it is a telling fact that Muslim detainees during the case, during the proceedings, pointed out that they lacked information, that they were not fully cognisant of the true state of affairs, and yet nevertheless, on the basis of their own observations, they came to conclusions that Milorad Krnojelac was merely a paper warden and that somebody else was responsible for them. And I should say that this should have been an alarming information for the Trial Chamber, necessitating the establishment of the true state of affairs in a different manner. Your Honours, if -- with your leave, if you have no questions in this regard, I would conclude with this, and, of course, once again I would refer to my appeal brief in which all the evidence and all the exhibits that I've touched upon are addressed in detail. We believe that if we take all this evidence altogether -- together and severally, all of this evidence can lead to only one conclusion and one conclusion only, that Milorad Krnojelac is not responsible for what went on in the Foca KP Dom. And now I'd like to move to ground 2 in the appeal brief of the Defence unless you want me to give you some additional explanations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I take it that it's your position that no reasonable trier of fact could come to the conclusion that Mr. Krnojelac was in fact the warden, and as you stated, you called him a paper warden. Could you please be so kind and explain what, based on your opinion, what would be the conclusion of a reasonable trier of fact based on the evidence from both sides during trial, what was his real role? Do you dispute he was there for 15 months? And what is, in your opinion, the work or what was the work of the accused when he spent these 15 months in KP Dom? What would you expect from the reasonable trier of fact?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with all due respect, it is my opinion that it is precisely this entire body of evidence that indicates that the KP Dom, apart from holding Muslim detainees, had certain capacities with an economic function. We have also demonstrated that the KP Dom had under its jurisdiction also 27 persons serving regular prison sentences. I therefore believe that based on this evidence, it would have been reasonable to determine, to find that the accused had no powers or jurisdiction over those other persons precisely because all the evidence and the exhibits that we have referred to. So, it is precisely the evidence that demonstrates that his duty and his function was to manage the economic unit, to manage that economic unit which even before the outbreak of the conflict was an important economic entity in Foca and continued in that role after the conflict broke out. Apart from managing the economic property and the economic unit which was the property of the KP Dom although it was physically leased, that economic unit continued to function and those 27 persons serving their regular prison sentences had been under his jurisdiction even before the outbreak of the conflict, and that was the essence of his duties in the course of those 15 months. I believe the entire body of evidence presents sufficient ground for such a finding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, you said, looking at the evidence, that it would have been reasonable for the Trial Chamber to find that your client did not have the authority in question. What my colleague Judge Schomburg put to you was this, that that was not really the question. The question was not whether it was reasonable for the Trial Chamber to find as it did but whether any reasonable Trial Chamber would have found otherwise. Now, take the evidence relating to a soldier telling the warden that he was not allowed to talk to a detainee and that the conversation was to be cut short. Now, you could argue from that that it showed that your client didn't have the authority in question. But was it open to the Trial Chamber to find otherwise? The Trial Chamber might have found that the soldier was not ordering the warden to discontinue the conversation but that the soldier was only reminding the warden of the proper position. What you have to argue is that the latter was not a conclusion which could have been drawn by any reasonable Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with all due respect, it is just the opinion of the Defence, and it is subject to your assessment and review. That is why we are here. I believe it would be really illogical and unusual for a simple guard to be reminding in such an insolent, I would say, way a warden about what is and what isn't permitted. I believe it is absolutely illogical under any legal system, and I think that it shows the absolute absence of actual control, actual power or actual superiority over such a person as this soldier. And if you allow me to add, I am not relying on one single exhibit. On the contrary, I have suggested that all the exhibits that I have referred to be viewed in combination. And it was a remark made by the Prosecution, which we accept, that one single exhibit, one single piece of evidence cannot demonstrate the real factual situation. That is why we suggested the entire body of evidence be viewed in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. If there are no other questions from my colleagues, we can move on to the second ground of appeal.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The second ground of appeal indicated by the Defence is the individual responsibility of the accused under Article 7(1) of the Statute of this Tribunal for aiding and abetting the crime of persecution as a crime against humanity based upon imprisonment and inhumane acts relating to living conditions. We believe that the Trial Chamber has erred in the application of law and in finding of facts when it found that the accused was individually responsible under Article 7(1) for aiding and abetting persecution as a crime against humanity based on imprisonment and inhumane acts related to living conditions. In its judgement, the Trial Chamber set out conditions for responsibility under Article 7(1) of the Statute and of individual responsibility under Article 7(3) of the Statute. And the Defence would not like to reiterate the standards set out by the Trial Chamber in its judgement. We believe that in making this erroneous conclusion, the Trial Chamber mainly relies upon and analyses only one of the essential elements for finding of this crime, that the Trial Chamber namely relies on the fact that the accused Krnojelac, as everyone else in the KP Dom, must have clearly understood that the main perpetrators of detention of Muslims and other non-Serbs had the intention of discriminating against these persons on religious and political grounds. However, the objection of the Defence would be that the Defence -- the Trial Chamber does not determine in a clear and unequivocal way that the accused was aware that his acts contribute to the commitment of the criminal act in question. The standard that should be applied, in my opinion, to find responsibility on this count, namely aiding and abetting, requires the existence of acts and omissions which constitute material assistance or support to the perpetrator in the commission of the crime. Also, participation and involvement in all this, in the opinion of the Defence and according to the established standards of this Tribunal, a participant or a supporter, that is the aider or abettor, must have significance influence on the commission of the crime, and his aiding and abetting must be real, actual, and substantial for the commission of the crime. Also, with reference to mens rea for aiding and abetting, it is essential that there be an intention to commit a crime or at least an awareness or a willingness to accept that the commission of the crime could be a possible consequence of one's acts or omissions. We believe that these standards for finding aiding and abetting in this case of the accused Krnojelac have not been determined clearly, and the conditions clearly set out for finding his criminal responsibility on this ground have not been met. So what are the acts and omissions that would have had substantial importance in aiding or abetting the perpetrators? In addition to establishing that, we believe it was essential to clearly establish the intention and willingness to aid and abet the perpetrators. We believe it is particularly necessary for the Trial Chamber to clearly and unequivocally identify the acts and omissions of the accused that significantly contributed to the perpetration of the criminal act upon discriminatory basis. We're speaking about the criminal act of imprisonment. In the case law of this Tribunal, we think that it has been clearly established and accepted that, as far as mens rea is concerned, a certain quality of mind set of the accused has to be more clearly shown. Invoking the case law, we further believe that the appeals judgement in the Kupreskic case established that aiding and abetting the perpetration of the crime of persecution requires one to prove that the accused has committed specific acts required to commit this crime or to support its commission. These acts also must have a significant influence on the commission of the crime of persecution, and the accused must, in addition, be aware that his acts contributed to persecution. In view of this ground of appeal and in view of the responsibility of the accused in aiding and abetting the criminal act of persecution as a crime against humanity, the Trial Chamber has not clearly and unequivocally established the responsibility of the accused, and we believe that a person who has been found in the judgement to lack a discriminatory mindset cannot be found at the same time to be an aider and abettor of discriminatory acts. Thus this begs a certain question. The Defence believes that the judgement of the Trial Chamber does not demonstrate which perpetrators of this crime Milorad Krnojelac significantly influenced by identifying his particular acts and omissions, especially if we bear in mind that even the Trial Chamber accepts that the accused Krnojelac had no participation or involvement in the act of imprisonment itself. Viewed through the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Agius has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Before you proceed on this particular point, because I think you're not being fair to the judgement of the Trial Chamber. I refer you specifically to paragraphs 318 and 319 of that judgement. The Trial Chamber did make a very clear distinction between certain guards of the KP Dom for whom your client was held to be responsible and other guards which were not under his direct command for whom he was not held to be responsible. And if you refer again to paragraph 318 of the same judgement, you see indicated in four subparagraphs numbered with Roman numbers i to iv -- i to v, the particular reasons on the basis of which the Trial Chamber decided that your client was responsible for having precisely aided and abetted those guards for whom he was responsible as far as the alleged crime of imprisonment is concerned. What you have to do state about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, of course I have read the judgement of the Trial Chamber, but in the humble opinion of this Defence counsel and in view of the standards that I have referred to, such findings are in our view insufficient to find the accused guilty of aiding and abetting these crimes precisely because we are talking about the crime of persecution which has a different mens rea to all the other criminal acts where in view of the Defence the aider and abettor must share the mens rea of the perpetrators. The aider and abettor almost shares in the crime itself. It is, as I've already said, the humble opinion of this Defence counsel, and it is precisely speaking about the crime of persecution that these findings are not sufficient for a finding of guilt. Thank you. I would conclude on this note my argumentation on the erroneous finding of guilt of the accused for aiding and abetting the crime of persecution, and in addition to all the other evidence during the trial, the Defence also provided an expert report demonstrating that the general economic conditions in Foca at the time were very poor, very poor indeed. I'm trying not to sound ironical. I respect everything that has been established and the suffering of the victims, but if we look at other camps, it has been established that in this camp three meals a day were provided. Again, I do not wish to sound ironical in the least, but efforts were made to provide a minimum of food and a minimum of hygiene. And we have, I believe, presented evidence that such efforts were indeed made. So this consciousness, awareness of discriminatory intent related to living conditions is very difficult to prove, and we believe that it has not been proven beyond reasonable doubt that the accused had the mens rea required for a finding of guilt of aiding and abetting persecution, and we believe the finding of the Trial Chamber is erroneous. And if you allow me, I will move on to the third ground of appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Shahabuddeen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I was interested in your proposition that an aider and abettor who shares in the intent of the principal parties almost shares in the crime itself. The point which is preoccupying me is this: Where do you draw the line, then, which separates the aider and abettor from the principal?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the distinction certainly must exist. When speaking of that, I didn't mean at all that this awareness, the intent and the willingness has to be of a scope that amounts to acceptance of the crime itself, but the Defence reasons with regard to aiding and abetting that if you support, aid somebody and abet them, we -- you have to share somebody's discriminatory intent. The distinction, of course, exists, but this standard for establishing responsibility under Article 7(1) for aiding and abetting must be viewed in a more narrow sense. It must be viewed through the prism of existence of discriminatory nature, discriminatory character of the aider and abettor himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've got five more minutes left, Mr. Bakrac. Would you like us to stop now or would you like to start with your third ground of appeal? As you prefer. I suggest we adjourn now and that we resume in half an hour. All right. Thank you. We are adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall resume. Could the accused please be led in. Mr. Bakrac, you have another hour, I think. Until noon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will move on to the next ground of appeal. And given that there are a number of points which form the basis of this ground of appeal, as for practical reasons this is how the Defence has presented them, I think we will have sufficient time to present in a concise manner what the position of the Defence is. The Trial Chamber failed to determine that the accused Krnojelac is guilty for the violation of the laws or customs of war based on living conditions both in accordance with responsibility according to 7(1) and in accordance to 7(3) of the Statute as a superior responsible for the acts of his subordinates. So the Trial Chamber determined that the accused was criminally responsible pursuant to 7(1) and 7(3) and to avail itself of its discretionary right to decide which basis of responsibility is more appropriate in order to attribute criminal responsibility to the accused. Thus, the Trial Chamber decided that the accused should be pronounced guilty for aiding and abetting of the main perpetrators, according to 7(1) of the Statute, and they added that his role as superior, the superior of those who were the direct perpetrators, this role would be considered as an aggravating factor in the decision on the appropriate sentence. When we turn to what the standards and what the tests are, the standards that have to be met if one is to decide that we're dealing with a criminal act or criminal responsibility according to 7(1) in terms of aiding and abetting, we believe that the Trial Chamber made a mistake when they decided that the accused was aware of the intent of the main perpetrators and, as warden, he was aware that by failing to act on his knowledge he significantly contributed to the perpetrators continuing to maintain the conditions, the perpetrators who committed cruel acts and inhumane acts. Thus, in this manner he contributed, he encouraged the perpetrators to maintain such living conditions, such cruel conditions. Naturally I don't want to burden the Appeal Chamber and I take into the third comment made with regard to presenting evidence that was presented in the course of the proceedings, so I will just point to the fact that there is evidence on the basis of which one could conclude that the Trial Chamber's findings were not reasonable when they decided on the responsibility of the accused. From the entire body of evidence, it is possible to single out certain evidence that brings into question, that casts down on the findings of the Trial Chamber and shows that there is reasonable doubt that the accused was aware that the inhumane conditions were the result of someone's intent and not because -- not the result of the actual situation during that period and in those circumstances in the territory concerned, and that he was in a position to improve those living conditions or at least he was aware that by failing to act he significantly contributed to the main perpetrators continuing to maintain those living conditions, thus he encouraged the perpetrators to maintain those conditions. I would also like to point out that in the light of these statements, these conclusions, there is evidence that the Defence has pointed out that shows that the conditions in the military part of the prison were established by the representatives of the military authorities, both with regard to accommodation, hygiene, and food for the detainees. I would like to refer to what the Defence mentioned in the first ground of appeal with regard to the material, written evidence that can support the position of the Defence. It is quite clear that with regard to the part of the KPD part where the detainees were kept, the military authorities had also been handed over the kitchen and the hospital. And according to Exhibit P2 included in the body of evidence by the Prosecution, that this is also evident. If we bear in mind and take into account this entire body of evidence, the conclusion we must inevitably reach is that -- or, rather, the question that one must pose is in such conditions, what could the accused Krnojelac have done? How could he have acted? He did not have the obligation -- according to the evidence we have referred to, he did not have the obligation of undertaking anything with regard to the living conditions of those persons who were in the part of the KPD that was within the grounds and under the command of the military authorities, the military command. If we add to this evidence the finding of the Trial Chamber that the accused Krnojelac did not have discriminatory intent and the evidence that was also included in the body of evidence and which -- which is the psychological report on the accused provided by both the Defence and the Prosecution and by the Prosecution's psychiatrist, if we take all of this into consideration, one can see that the accused Krnojelac has such a personality, such a character that he does not have any such discriminatory intent, which would be the main pre-supposition to claim that there were such crimes based on racial, religious, or racial -- or racial definitions. There is also a series -- there's also a number of pieces of evidence that show that the accused, given his position in the KPD and given the duties he had to perform, although he was not responsible for the living conditions, he attempted to improve those living conditions. And it was established, it seems, that this intention to obtain extra food, we have evidence of Bozidar Drakul and we have Exhibit D107 which shows that when he contacted the International Red Cross with regard to the Serbs who were serving their sentence, he informed them that there were also Muslim detainees in the KPD and requested additional food for them too, additional supplies. And it seems that these facts, instead of improving the position as far as criminal responsibility is concerned of the accused, it seems that these facts have been treated as evidence on the part of the Trial Chamber to show that the accused was responsible for taking action to improve the living conditions of the non-Serb detainees. So with regard to the intention and although he was not obliged to improve the living conditions, with regard to the intention to improve the living conditions, the witness Divljan Lazar referred to in the appeal brief by the Defence, and we have also referred to Exhibit 146, it's Divljan Lazar's diary which he kept as the person responsible for the warehouse in the KPD. It shows that everything that was issued, all the hygienic items and food issued to non-Serbian detainees, it mentions all these items that were issued to non-Serbian detainees. The question is that given these facts, the accused attempted to take action, attempted to perform certain tasks that were not really his responsibility. He attempted to improve the situation, but this has been interpreted as something that shows that he had an obligation to improve conditions and he failed to fulfil these obligations as he should have done as warden responsible for the situation in peacetime, before the conflict broke out. If one takes into consideration that such an intent can -- existed, then with all the evidence, it's not possible to claim that the accused Krnojelac was aware of the situation, if we bear in mind the economic situation, the fact that the accused took items from the KPD warehouse and provided hygienic items and food. And according to one of the Prosecution's witnesses, some of the food produced on the farm was also provided to the KPD. So given these facts, the question one must ask is: Where is one to locate the intent? How can one demonstrate that the accused Krnojelac wanted to facilitate the perpetration of such acts and wanted to contribute to maintaining inhuman living conditions? How can one say that he accepted the maintenance of such conditions? What sort of behaviour are we referring to? How did he significantly aid and abet the principal perpetrators to continue committing such acts? We believe that on the basis of all these facts, on the basis of all the evidence that we have referred to, not a single reasonable Trial Chamber could reach the conclusion that the accused significantly contributed to the maintenance of these living conditions or to the deterioration of such living conditions. By his acts or omissions, they cannot show by his acts or omissions he aided and abetted the main perpetrators to maintain such living conditions. Given time restrictions and the promise I made, I would like to turn to the following ground of appeal, and at the end we will -- we suggest that the decision should be revised on this count 2 and the accused should not be considered responsible on this count. With your permission, I would now like to move on to the following ground of appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Perhaps in general terms, to have a careful look at the judgement on each occasion, because you see your accused was held responsible as an accomplice and as a superior, as an aider and abettor and a superior. And you mentioned all the evidence provided to the Trial Chamber in many paragraphs. I think it starts in paragraph 140 of the judgement, and these are the essential points. Naturally it's an error of fact that you are indicating, but it has a double imputation, a double significance on the part of the Trial Chamber. So please bear in mind what role of the Appeals Chamber is. Thank you. If you have nothing -- if there is nothing else, we can move on to the following point.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. With regard to that comment, I just wanted to say that as far as responsibility on the basis of 7(3) with regard to command responsibility, that remains as it was. As far as the fourth ground of appeal is concerned, we consider that the Trial Chamber failed to establish that -- they made an error when they found that he was responsible in accordance with 7(1) for persecution as a crime against humanity on the basis of beatings according to count 1 in the indictment. We don't want to repeat everything on which the Defence has spent a lot of time in order to establish the position of the accused. We think that all the evidence and all the factual errors we have pointed to, we think that this is also significant for this basis, that is to say the possibility for the appropriateness of deeming that Krnojelac, the accused, is responsible for the crimes committed by his subordinates. And the Trial Chamber found that the subordinates were the prison guards who participated directly in the perpetration of these acts. I would also like to emphasise that factual error was made, especially with regard -- especially with regard to establishing the nature of the authority, the nature of the hierarchy within which these prison guards functioned. So we support the ground of appeal number 1 with regard to which we used much evidence and the testimony of guard -- of prison guards to show that these guards had been appointed by the military command and they were directly responsible to the military command. They were subordinated to the military command. So each incident, each excessive act committed by prison guards in the KPD is not something for which the accused could be held responsible on the basis of command responsibility. In the judgement of the Trial Chamber, the basis for such a finding is provided by three examples, three examples that -- of which the accused Krnojelac could have been aware. So in addition to these three -- in addition to these main objections that the prison guards were not employed by the Ministry of Justice and were not the subordinates of the accused Krnojelac another question we must ask is whether the accused Krnojelac had a sufficient amount of alarming information which would lead him to find out about the perpetration of such criminal acts and which would incite him to launch an investigation into such incidents and into the perpetrators of these acts. So with regard to this ground and with regard to the comment of the President of the Appeals Chamber, I would not like to repeat arguments that we have already made. I would just like to remind you that the Defence yesterday when presenting its case and responding to the Prosecution's brief discussed these three examples that the Trial Chamber took into account when it found that the accused Krnojelac could have known and had reason to know that there were beatings in the KPD, beatings in which the prison guards participated. These are examples that include Ekrem Zekovic. And we have said that this happened at the very end of the accused's term in the KPD. And then in addition to all the other comments we've made in this part of our brief, we have the example of the witness RJ. And as to whether there is evidence that these beatings were carried out on a discriminatory basis, that is something that we have also discussed. In addition, we think that to establish such responsibility it is important to demonstrate the existence of effective control that the accused had over these persons. For this reason, we believe that this finding reached by the Trial Chamber is erroneous and it ought to be changed. If it is not necessary to provide any other information or any other explanations, the Defence would like to move on to the following ground of appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, you have dwelt on the scope of the appellant's authority, and you have submitted that the prison guards were appointed by the -- I think the military authorities and were not in any sense the subordinates of your client. Did your client have any functions in relation to the prison guards, or alternatively, did the prison guards discharge any duties in relation to your client? I just don't know. I -- I wait on your reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence is only referring to what is part of the facts of the case. We have three or four guards who during the relevant period of time were present in the KPD, and they testified before the Trial Chamber and stated that they had been appointed by the military command of the Foca Tactical Group and that they received orders from the military command and that they spent some time standing guard in the KPD and another part of their time going to the front. Mile Matovic, one of the guards, also provided documents to this effect, documents in which this is supported. And the Defence has included this among its exhibits. I apologise. I don't want to waste time now to try and find this. In the written brief of the Defence, we have the reference. When the Defence said that not a single reasonable Trial Chamber could reach the conclusion that the accused Krnojelac actually had effective control, the Defence wanted to -- was thinking of all of the evidence, was referring to all evidence, including the evidence presented by the Prosecution. There is not a single piece of evidence that demonstrates that anyone saw or heard the accused Krnojelac issuing orders to the guards within the KPD. So this is the basis on which the Defence claims that the accused did not have command responsibility. In other words, that he was not the superior of these guards. My apologies. The exhibit to which I'm referring, for the record, is D151. May I move on? The Trial Chamber was also wrong when it found guilty the accused Milorad Krnojelac as superior for inhuman acts as a crime against humanity, and cruel treatment as a violation of the laws or customs of war both based on beatings, under Article 7(3). So as in the case of our previous ground for appeal, in the case of this one, the Defence objects to this finding and says that the Trial Chamber relied on three beatings which the Trial Chamber thought that the accused knew or could have known about had he been performing his duties. Now, the objection in which we submit that the chain of command, the hierarchy, or the absence of the duty to prevent or punish prison guards has already been made by the Defence and we don't want to waste any of our precious time to go into it once again. Likewise, in the exhibits, the evidence on the basis of which the Trial Chamber found that fact includes those which the Defence has already pointed out at when it disputed or, rather, challenged the fact that the accused had enough knowledge or that he was in a position that he was aware of these acts and that his position would allow him to initiate action against such persons or to initiate the investigation. With regard to his command responsibility, we think that all the objections that we already pointed out hold true once again as in the previous grounds of appeal. So we merely erred that there is -- there is no subordination, there is no hierarchy there or any kind of effective control chain that would allow him to either investigate acts of those persons or to punish them in the light of the position that Krnojelac held. I also think that one of the examples on which the Trial Chamber relied on in its judgement and that concerns the beating of Ekrem Zekovic, which happened as he turned up, shows the absence of any form of authority or effective control over these persons. In addition to the objection -- in addition to the comment that the Defence has also tendered into evidence, the decision of the Ministry of Justice relieving the accused of the duty of the warden of the KP Dom as of the 1st of July - and this incident happened on the 9th - we simply think that the Trial Chamber went wrong because the conduct of a guard in the presence -- in front of the accused could be indicative of the fact that he did not have any practical control or that he -- that -- and showed that he did not enjoy any authority in relation to those guards even though perhaps the position might presume it. And we therefore think that this finding of the Trial Chamber was erroneous and that the accused should be acquitted of responsibility under this count of the indictment. And once again, I'm trying to avoid being repetitive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Counsel. This is merely the information. Where, in what do you find this contradiction? You talk about the incident with Ekrem Zekovic and you're saying that he was no longer a warden, but when he was a warden, then does it not implicitly mean that he was responsible? So my second question is: Did he conduct an investigation?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence believes that even when he was the warden he was not -- he did not have that responsibility for reasons that we've already indicated. The Defence mentioned this example merely to support its argument, to corroborate its submissions. In addition to all our submissions that he wasn't really their warden and that he wasn't their superior, we are trying to show with this example of a guard who really couldn't care less that a warden is right next to him and that he is engaged in a punishable act. We think that this shows that in spite of the formal condition which was already seized, that is he was no longer a superior there, he couldn't punish, but the very conduct of that guard on the ground shows that he was aware, that he realised that the accused was not the person who could punish him or who had any such authority, that he was not the person who was his superior. So that shows that even before that -- I'm trying to answer your question -- that even before that, he did not have any instruments at his disposal which would allow him to punish the perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Just to clear my mind, Mr. Bakrac, you're putting your case this way: Apropos of this conversation between the guard and your client, I understand you to be saying that there was no material basis on which the Trial Chamber could find against your proposition that that evidence showed that your client did not have the authority in question, that no reasonable Trial Chamber could interpret the evidence differently, that no reasonable Trial Chamber, for example, could say, "Well, this soldier wasn't giving orders to the warden but was merely reminding the warden of the exact position." You say no reasonable Trial Chamber could have so concluded. Do I understand your case correctly?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. With all due respect, I owe you an explanation. Once again, not in isolation. Of course, that one example isolated from other examples and evidence cannot show that no reasonable tribunal of fact would have decided as it did. I'm simply trying to put together the picture, the whole mosaic of evidence corroborating the Defence's position that all these testimonies and evidence when put together give us a picture which showed that a decision on the responsibility or the existence of the chain of command in the sense in which it was talking existed and that that was why the accused should have been found guilty. May I move on? I -- and our last ground of appeal, ground of appeal of the Defence, is the sentence. I'd like to apologise in advance to the Appeals Chamber for possibly misinterpretation of the discretionary rights of the Appeals Chamber with regard to the decision on the sentence, because perhaps it arises from the characteristics of the legal system that I come from where this kind of objections is possible. So please accept my apologies if I go slightly beyond the scope of the discretionary rights of the Chamber. However, I hope you will allow me to articulate them because I think if we are to be fair to the accused, then perhaps you should hear something which perhaps does not make part of the standard, but the Defence nevertheless believes could help the accused and help you understand the degree of his criminal responsibility or his participation under either 7(1) or aiding and abetting or 7(3), that is crimes that are laid at his door. We, namely, believe that the Trial Chamber found correctly or, rather, showed that the standard in weighing the sentence was an imperative duty, that on the one hand the sentence was meted out in fairness to the circumstances of the accused and the gravity of the crimes that he stands accused of. As for the former, the Defence does not think that the Trial Chamber fully went beyond its discretionary right and disregarded completely quite a number of personal circumstances which would go in favour of the accused. We simply think that some of his personal circumstances and the Defence believes with all due modesty that they should be taken into account when determining the final judgement. We think that these circumstances were not accorded proper weight. It is correct that the Trial Chamber, in its decision, addressed the age of the accused Krnojelac. He is 62 years old and that was taken into account. But we also think, however, that the Trial Chamber could have, when drawing a parallel among three similar cases, omitted when determining the sentence in these three cases, we believe that it omitted to take into account the age. In our case, it is much more advanced and in the other two cases that were used in comparison. It is a fact, if we are talking about personal circumstances, that again in relation to the age, that the numerous family that the accused has, four sons, two of whom are disabled, one lost both his legs, one lost one leg during this unfortunate war in the territory of Foca. And for grandchildren, two or three of whom the accused has never seen because he's been in detention. This should also make up part of the personal circumstances which we believe the Trial Chamber did not sufficiently bear in mind. Personal circumstances also include, in the Defence's opinion a well known fact which is indisputable, and that is that the accused from the beginning of his career has worked as a mathematics teacher with children in the elementary school, and this period of 15 months is the only period when he was placed under labour obligation, that is, under wartime assignment when he was assigned to that post. And he had absolutely no previous experience in that regard. Another thing which we believe should be accorded to your attention is the conduct of the accused. We think that the sentence does not properly reflect the level, the gravity of the criminal conduct of the accused. When we look at all the grounds of criminal liability and the crimes of which he stands accused and the significant contribution, that is all the significance contributions, all that we have said about his contribution to the acts, we think that all this was not properly assessed, properly appraised by the Trial Chamber. The Defence cannot help but think that the criminal gravity of the accused could come back to one sentence which the Trial Chamber said, he decided to act like an ostrich. And we think if the Appeals Chamber decides that the Trial Chamber acted correctly in assessing the criminal liability of the accused, then his overall crime conduct could be -- could come down to that one sentence, that he chose to put his head in the sand. In the body of evidence, you cannot find a single fact proving that during that 15 months time the accused ever cast an ugly look at a detained Muslim or non-Serb let alone used inappropriate vocabulary when addressing such a detainee. Quite the contrary. We have the testimony of a witness for the Prosecution who, even though he lost a son in the KP Dom, said in the court, he said that this accused treated Muslims amicably. So when we speak about his overall criminal conduct and its gravity, there I think, of course, and far about it from me to show disrespect for the victims, far be it from me to bring to question his criminal responsibility, if you find he was indeed criminally responsible, we think that one should bear in mind the minimum of participation, that is if he chose to put his head in the sand, that is, his omission to act, we think that if you find him criminally responsible, that omission should be the only criminal responsibility that he could and should be sentenced for. Under the conditions when the Trial Chamber found that the accused was criminally responsible, I would still think that that decision was inadequate and that it should be reversed. In the decision, in the judgement, the Trial Chamber seized upon its right and drew comparison with similar cases, but the thing that the Prosecution also addressed to this appeal refers to the length of time that the accused spent in the KP Dom. When we talk about two similar cases, Aleksovski and Mucic, we have five, that is seven, that is 15 months. You would have a much shorter period of time in the Kvocka case. But what one has to look at, the substance of the matter when weighing up the sentence, is not the duration, is not the length of time but the overall amount of crimes, the number of crimes that happened during that time. Out of respect for the victims and out -- my professional attitude towards other cases, I do not want to compare a camp that existed for four months only, but there you will see more crimes happening than over 15 months' time. The length of time should not be a yardstick, a measure. What should be a measure is what happened during the relevant period. I think that it is even aggravating if more crimes happened during a shorter period of type. I think it should be an aggravating circumstance for the one who is found liable for that particular period. And I would like also to add one comment of the Defence with regard to that matter, the length of time. If somebody during 15 months that he spent surrounded by Serbs who are discriminated against, and if he managed not even to cast an ugly look at any one of them, then that, I think, tells us about his nature, about his non-discriminatory nature and about his disagreement with what was going on. And I ask of the Chamber that that 15 months which the Prosecution insists upon, which is also underlined in the judgement, I do ask the Appeals Chamber to appraise it correctly and accept the Defence's explanation. What I have said now, and I hope you won't misunderstand it, you won't take it wrongly, this is merely how the Defence sees it, because we're trying to present to you our viewpoint the way in which we believe should one interpret the length of time that the accused spent in the KP Dom. We therefore stand by all our grounds of appeal that we presented in our brief. And if the Appeals Chamber establishes that there is no responsibility under any count, we propose that the accused be acquitted. And if the Appeals Chamber establishes that the Trial Chamber was right under all counts, nevertheless we ask the Appeals Chamber to -- to sentence him to a lighter term because we think that this and the current sentence is too severe. And if you do find him indeed guilty - and we do not think he is - then we hope that he will receive a milder sentence from you. That is all that we wish to stay to the Appeals Chamber at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are there any questions? Well, right. Thank you. You're finished within your time limit. Well, the Judges have decided that the break will be between 12.30 and 14.00, so that the Prosecutor, you may start with your reply and we shall make our break at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. May it please the Chamber. Yesterday the Prosecution presented its arguments in the Prosecution appeal. Today it presents its arguments in response to the Defence appeal. And the Prosecution is now in the somewhat curious position that in this Defence appeal it is defending aspects of the Trial Chamber's judgement that yesterday it sought to challenge in the Prosecution appeal. In particular, yesterday the Prosecution argued that the Trial Chamber erred in holding the appellant individually responsible for certain crimes as an aider and abettor, the Prosecution position being that he should have been held liable for committing those crimes as a participant in a joint criminal enterprise. Today, in response to the Defence appeal, the Prosecution is arguing that the Trial Chamber committed no error in finding the appellant to be an aider and abettor. This situation is not illogical in situations where both parties appeal against a judgement of a Trial Chamber.
