On the one hand, the Prosecution -- in the Prosecution appeal, the Prosecution is arguing that the Trial Chamber should have gone further than it did in determining the individual criminal responsibility of the appellant. On the other hand, in the Defence appeal, the Prosecution is arguing that it did not commit any error in going at least to the extent that it did. And if the Appeals Chamber did not uphold the Prosecution's first ground of appeal, the Prosecution's submission is that the convictions as an aider and abettor should stand. Thus when in its response now to the Defence appeal the Prosecution argues that there was no error in holding the appellant to be an aider and abettor, the Prosecution is not thereby resiling in any way from the position that it took yesterday. It is simply the case that for the purposes of responding to the Defence appeal, the Prosecution must, for the time being, put its own appeal to one side. Nevertheless, to avoid any confusion or appearance of inconsistency, the Appeals Chamber may be assisted by some introductory submissions on the relationship between the Prosecution appeal and the Prosecution response to the Defence appeal. There is a certain overlap in the arguments in the two appeals. For instance, in relation to his individual criminal liability under Article 7(1) for imprisonment and living conditions, a principal line of argument by the Defence in its second ground of appeal is that the Prosecution has failed to identify specific acts of specific principal offenders and has failed to identify specific acts of the appellant which are said to have aided and abetted those acts by the principal offenders. As a general response to this line of argument, I would recall the submission that I made yesterday. In relation to the unlawful imprisonment, the Prosecution submits that even on the facts as found by the Trial Chamber, it's clear from paragraph 127 of the trial judgement that the Trial Chamber found that this imprisonment was effected by a joint criminal enterprise. As I said yesterday, the Trial Chamber in that paragraph refers to "the joint criminal enterprise" and to "that joint criminal enterprise" and to "the unlawful system." And the only question, in our submission, was whether the appellant was a participant in that joint criminal enterprise or whether he was an aider and abettor to the joint criminal enterprise or whether, as the Defence now submits, he had no criminal liability at all. The Trial Chamber found him to be an aider and abettor, which is to say that he was an aider and abettor to a joint criminal enterprise. The Prosecution submitted in its appeal that he was a participant in the joint criminal enterprise, but as I say, I've put that to one side for now. For purposes of the Defence appeal, a question is whether in order to convict an accused as an aider and abettor of a joint criminal enterprise, is it necessary to identify specific acts of specific participants in that enterprise that the accused has aided and abetted? And the Prosecution's submission is that in cases of the second category of joint criminal enterprise, that cannot be the case. The second category, as I've said, is the category of systemic joint criminal enterprises in which even the participants may not be aware of each other's identities. What is required is knowledge of the system and of the common plan, design, or purpose which it's intended to give effect. The Prosecution position is that the appellant made a substantial contribution to the system of unlawful confinement by acting as the most senior figure within the prison for 15 months, with the requisite knowledge of the unlawful system and of the contribution that he was thereby making to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: The Prosecution's apologies yet again to the translators. It's unnecessary, in the Prosecution's submission, to show that the appellant's acts in some more particular way aided and abetted, say, a particular prison guard to commit a particular act of mistreatment on a particular day. In relation to the inhumane living conditions in the camp, the Trial Chamber made no finding that there was a joint criminal enterprise, although, perhaps significantly, it also made no finding that there was not. The relevant paragraph is paragraph 170. The trial judgement might even be read as implicitly finding that there was a joint criminal enterprise with respect to the inhumane living conditions and found that the appellant was only an aider and abettor to that. I referred yesterday to a number of paragraphs in the trial judgement, finding that the inhumane conditions were the result of deliberate policies. As I submitted yesterday, it's evident that deliberate policies of the kind found by the Trial Chamber cannot have been the result of the actions of a single person or of a number of different persons acting independently of each other. Such deliberate policies could only be the result of a number of persons acting in concert in a joint enterprise. However, even assuming that the Trial Chamber's judgement cannot be read as making any such finding, and even assuming that it made no finding of a joint criminal enterprise in relation to the imprisonment, it's submitted that if deliberate policies were being implemented in a systematic way by principal offenders to imprison and impose inhumane living conditions on detainees in a prison, the appellant, by discharging his responsibilities as warden and failing to take action to prevent the crimes being committed there, was clearly contributing substantially to the ability of the principal offenders to implement those deliberate policies. There can be no detention without a prison and a prison cannot exist and function without administration, and that important requirement was being provided by the appellant, in the Trial Chamber's findings. Similarly, unless they had been confined in the prison, they could not have been subjected to the deliberate policies of inhumane conditions. On the requirements for aiding and abetting, it has been held in the case law of this Tribunal that it's not necessary that the aider and abettor should know the precise crime that was intended and which in the event was committed, if he's aware that one of a number of crimes will probably be committed and one of those crimes is in fact committed, he has intended to facilitate the commission of that crime and is guilty as an aider and abettor. For that proposition, I would refer to the Furundzija trial judgement, paragraph 246, the Blaskic trial judgement, paragraph 287, and the Tuta and Stela trial judgement at paragraph 63 and in the Tadic appeal judgement, paragraph 227(ii), it was held that the principal may not know even of the accomplice's contribution. It's therefore unnecessary to the Prosecution's submission to show that the appellant's acts in some more particular way aided and abetted, say, a pick prison guard to commit a particular act of mistreatment on a particular day. Your Honour Judge Shahabuddeen, during the presentation of the Defence arguments, asked a question at the point of which aiding and abetting becomes participation in the crime itself. We addressed that question yesterday. I won't repeat the Prosecution's submissions, but I would just recall again our submission that there is a difference between motive and intent. And in fact, a person who is contributing significantly to a crime, for instance in a system of mistreatment, the most effective, the most active cog in the machine may in fact be doing what he's doing for motive such as to receive promotion in the system without actually wishing any ill-will on the victims. The intent comes from the intent to participate in the enterprise rather than from the motive of achieving the result of the enterprise. With those introductory comments, the Prosecution would now turn to address the specific grounds of appeal of the Defence in turn. We have provided the Chamber with an order of appearance again. I would first invite the Chamber to call upon my colleague Mr. Carmona to address the Defence's grounds 1 and parts of grounds 3 and grounds 4 which relate to the appellant's position as warden. He would be followed by Ms. Rashid who will address Defence grounds 2 and 3, followed by Ms. Brady who will address grounds 4 and grounds 5, and, finally, I will conclude by presenting the Prosecution's submissions on the Defence ground 6 relating to sentence. I would invite the Presiding Judge to call on my colleague Mr. Carmona.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do take the admonition that was mentioned yesterday with regard to the need to be precise and also, in fact, not to regurgitate facts for the purposes of this appeal and more so for the purposes of this response. But I think it is pertinent to make certain observations with regard to what my learned colleague has said, and in this regard, it is the intention of the Prosecution to respond both globally and specifically as it pertains to the material areas of contention and in terms of the importance to a proper determination of the assessment of the Trial Chamber's judgement. Apart from that, one has to make some preliminary observations, and that is as Kupreskic, as Celebici have both indicated that it is not the prerogative of the Defence to simply regurgitate arguments that are in fact in their final trial briefs without in fact showing more, without showing, for example, that it represents an unreasonable finding and that an unreasonable finding has resulting in an error of fact, resulting in a miscarriage of justice. Because it would have the undesirable effect of not providing the Appeals Chamber with its mandate which is, in fact, one of corrective nature and would result in a de novo hearing and reassessment of facts found by the Trial Chamber. So I take this very broad, this very broad imperative when, for example, I am dealing with the facts. Additionally, I wish to note that as much as, in fact, the Defence has focused on various strands of evidence to illustrate and to support its arguments, that the Prosecution in its brief has always, in fact, held that what is required is an in toto evaluation of the evidence and not a dissemination or, rather, I should say a splitting of individual strands of evidence for the purpose of the exercise of this appeal. I dare say my learned colleague has indeed made a concession this morning that he agrees with, in fact, the appeals to the Prosecution's approach that what that is in fact required is a more broad-based total assessment of the evidence as a whole in, in fact, the evaluation process. It is my intention, however, in dealing with this collective approach to maintain at all times that it is not the responsibility, neither is it in fact the mandate of the Prosecution to address every single microscopic evaluation done in relation to every single strand of evidence. And this is why I indicated that, in fact, we will do it both globally and specifically, contingent on what the need is in the context of the judgement. I will begin by referring specifically to areas -- some of those areas broached by my friend as areas of concern. Specifically, it is the submission of the Prosecution that he has not, in fact, shown that the Trial Chamber was unreasonable in its findings. He indicated very categorically that the position of warden is crucial and critical to an assessment of his client's liability. This particular point was very much in the forefront of the Trial Chamber's mind. In fact, at paragraph 90, at note 278, the Trial Chamber recognised that in its opening salvo, the Defence, in fact, made mention that he was attacking formally and factual the findings with regard to the position of warden in the -- in this particular -- in this particular case. And in so doing, he indicated further that he would in fact bring evidence to illustrate his arguments. I think it is pertinent that I refer to that particular document without going into it extensively yesterday, where attempts were made by the Defence at trial to tender a document dated 11th of January, 2000, from the Ministry of Defence, a certificate which in fact was a summary of data looked at by the said -- the Defence Ministry and which was indicating that the only responsibility of, in fact, Krnojelac, the appellant, was one for the protection of provisions or protection of property at the KP Dom. When, for example, the Trial Chamber raised the issue of weight - not admissibility but weight - he indicated in fact that he would tender documents subsequently to illustrate his point, to confirm his point. And at the end of the day, even though, for example, he was given this opportunity, that certificate was not tendered. There was no request to tender that into evidence, and there was none of those documents that, in fact, he promised forthcoming. It is significant to note that the Prosecution, when it attempted to cross-examine on the particular document that my learned colleagues in fact on the other side indicated that this document is not in evidence. And based on its assessment of the fact they were not able to tender certain material but more specifically based on the affirmative evidence led by the Prosecution that came to the conclusion that the position, authority, and status of Krnojelac was far more than one responsible for safeguarding property. In addition, we have the evidence of FWS-138 who in fact was an in a very peculiar position, unlike most of those detainees, and he in fact gave very pertinent evidence with regard to the maintenance of the structure within the camp pre- and post- the conflict. Because, Your Honours, this particular witness was in fact a guard at the camp pre-conflict, before it became the camp that it was. Ironically, he found himself in the camp as a detainee. So he was in a position to assess and evaluate, and give a level of credence to the whole structure as envisaged, as he knew, as he practiced when he was there before and when he is there now. And the thing is that the Trial Chamber placed a lot of reliance on his observations based on the experience that he had been a former camp guard. And this is, in fact, seen in paragraph 102 at note 302. And in particular with regard to the role of -- the role of Krnojelac in the context of responsibilities vis-a-vis the guards. He said very categorically at T2030 to D2034, the warden had the Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 263 to 271. obligation to report serious beating of an inmate by a guard to the Ministry of Justice. And the bottom line is, at the end of the day, that when you are referring - and I will be doing this extensively - when you are dealing with 7(3) responsibility, we need to consider that a lot of these organisations and defences -- the ministries operating outside the camp were very fluid. The bottom line is in fact there was a state of administrative fluidity in Foca where in fact there was liaising between the defence of Justice, the defence of Defence, the defence of economy. And we must not in fact get into the difficulty of artificially dividing the ministries as if in fact they operated singularly and apart given in fact what was taking place at the time. When one looks, for example, at the Gazette that indicated the appointment of Krnojelac on the 17th of June, 1992, it spoke, for example, that the prison warden was responsible for the internal management of the prison. It also told significantly -- and this is an example of how in fact these organisations were so volatile: It mentions that the security of the prison shall be provided by employees working in institutions, and if necessary - if necessary - employees of MUP, the Ministry of the Interior, and police. So that in fact is it was -- it was a case where, for example, the entire supervisory responsibility was not one that was in fact simply restricted to the guards themselves, again, because of the level of fluidity operating within the system. And this can be gleaned from the Gazette of the 12th to the 17th of May, 1992. Apart from that, apart from these administrative indicators of the relationship among the various ministries, there was evidence also from various witnesses. For example, FWS-214 and FWS-139, who indicated that when they complained to Mitar Rasevic, in fact who was the commander to the guards, with regard to the conditions, the living conditions in the camp, and more significantly, the beatings, he indicated very categorically that in fact you would have to speak to the warden about that. My learned friend has indicated, has respond -- has made reference to a document P2, and indicates, for example, that this document that was forwarded to the Ministry of Justice as an indicator that, for example, the kitchen and the hospital beds were handed over to the Tactical Foca Group. But the bottom line is in fact that these particular organisations, if I may so call it, the kitchen and the hospital, was responsible for all the detainees in the camp. There was no kind of divisive responsibility. Apart from that, when, for example, reference is made to Zoran Zekovic who in fact was the new prison warden who took over from Krnojelac at the end of his stint at the end of July 1993, and in fact he was called upon the Ministry of Justice to indicate exactly the workers who worked from 1992 to 1993, and he refers to Zoran Zekovic as some kind of legal assistant. And they are using this as the basis for saying, for example, that it shows, for example, that the warden in fact didn't have -- didn't have any clout. But what it shows, very matter-of-factly, is that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: My apologies. What it shows is that Todovic was in fact a subordinate -- Savo Todovic was the subordinate to Krnojelac. Yes, I know we have heard about in fact Krnojelac being a paper warden and being a paper tiger, if I may so describe it, but it is the position of the Prosecution, as found by the facts in the Trial Chamber's judgement, that he was not. Mention was made additionally to D85, and it was indicated that this represented the scope of his duties as warden. Again, in fact, this is a document that dealt with the lease agreement, and as much as in fact, for example, this lease agreement is a bone of contention, the arguments raised by my learned friend on the other side is ad idem with his brief, and we have responded in extenso to that argument, and we stand by that, by those arguments. Additionally -- and this is in fact something that in fact we have mentioned in, in fact, our opening salvo with regard to what is the mandate of the Appeals Chamber. My friend has made mention of six individuals who in fact suffered from some drug addiction and who in fact, for example, were placed inside the KP Dom and were somehow in fact placed with the non-Serb detainees, et cetera. The mention of this is coming about for the first time in the appeal. On the record, there is nothing to indicate what this is all about. Apart from that, when one looks at my learned friend's brief, it is just a blanket statement made there, and Kunarac has said very categorically you simply cannot put forward factual matters without showing the relationship of these factual matters to in fact errors of fact resulting with a miscarriage of justice. And if in fact you do this, it will be rejected. Another very important feature with regard to the role, status, and position and power of the individual concerned is that Krnojelac, by his own admission, because much has been said about the Drina Economic Unit, by his own admission when giving evidence admitted that in fact he was a warden and he was also the director of the Drina Economic Unit. Now, if you are giving evidence and you basically in fact categorise your position in the context of two different positions, isn't it an indicator that you do in fact wield authority; that you do wield authority in relation to the Drina Economic Unit and you do wield authority as prison warden. But what is even more significant, and it has to do with regard to the argument that in terms of his responsibilities and his power and control over the guards, is that he also gave evidence that guards, in fact, who were in charge of the Drina Economic Unit were also guards who were also in charge of the non-Serb detainees. And to the extent that in fact that he in fact has a dual type of responsibility, you're talking about two limbs of authority to deal with those guards; limbs of authority to deal with them as prison warden and limbs of authority to deal with them as director of the Drina Economic Unit. But then again, when looking at my friend's argument, he has made heavy weather of the fact that there are a lot of documents that -- of requests from Krnojelac to various ministries, more specifically, the Ministry of the Economy. What in fact my friend in fact does not do, however, is explain how it is, for example, that you are maintaining that you are just simply a prison guard without -- without any kind of decisive function yet you are sending a memo to the War Presidency indicating very categorically that in fact security needs to be beefed up, that in fact that you advise that mines be placed to prevent the detainees from escaping. And the thing about this is that in fact when you send that letter, this is a follow-up letter to the one written on the 1st of June, 1992, requesting the same laying of mines within the section of KP Dom. He writes to the Ministry of the Economy indicating that he needed 20 tons of oil for the purposes again of production and security. And there is evidence from various witnesses that in fact while these mines were in fact being laid, it was done by soldiers in the presence of Krnojelac. And this makes me make the point, that a Trial Chamber does not have the responsibility to articulate every factual finding in its -- and have it put in its judgement. One would expect as reasonable assessor of the Trial Chamber's position that if, for example, they make mention of a particular fact, they make mention of the 20 tons of oil, they make mention of the fact that he wrote to the Ministry of the War Presidency asking for mines, and there is evidence, for example, that he's in the company of soldiers while these mines are being put down, isn't it in fact -- is it not reasonable to conclude that they would have been, in fact, privy and take cognisance of all that evidence? Again, too, when one looks at Exhibit -- Defence Exhibit 83A, Defence Exhibit 39A, these are in fact indicia of the nature and scope of authority that he was in possession of. Now, much -- additional my -- additionally my friend made mention of the fact that Krnojelac he came to work from 7 to 3. There is evidence that, in fact, he came from 7 to 4. There is also evidence that, in fact, he was seen in the evenings. The bottom line is he came to work every single day. The bottom line is that, in fact, the only time when there was some kind of absence or aberration in terms of presence was when he went to see about his son in Belgrade on the 24th of June, 1992, who had, in fact, suffered some terrible wounds, and he was aware for approximately seven days until the 2nd and 3rd of July. In Celebici, Mucic, by virtue of his deportment, absented himself at various times, on various occasions, from the prison, and the Trial Chamber was of the view that this was irrelevant to the whole concept of 7(3). More so in the fact that he was there for seven months, and in the case of Krnojelac, you were there for 15. This was referred, in fact, to by arguments in relation to superior responsibility yesterday, and I stand by those by those particular arguments. Now, much has been mentioned also of the appointment of Krnojelac and the voluntariness of that appointment. The Prosecution, in fact, led evidence -- I will close up on this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I just wish -- I just wish to remind the honourable quorum that I am also in fact dealing with ground -- the third ground of appeal, subground 2, and also in fact the fourth ground of appeal, which in fact is subground two also. And they all, of course, relate to his position and role of authority as KP Dom warden. So basically it's almost like a global approach to the particular areas of contention. At the break, in fact, I was just about to mention that the Trial Chamber, according to the appellant, had more or less in fact -- had placed emphasis on the evidence of -- of Tesovic and Veselin Cancar as a basis for saying that the voluntariness of the appointment of Krnojelac was indeed voluntary and, therefore, there was no basis for questioning it. I dare say, in fact, we have outlined in our arguments in the brief our response to my learned friend's arguments, and we stand by those. Additionally, in relation to the whole issue with regard to Krnojelac indicating that he in fact felt threatened by the appointment, there is in fact no evidence according to -- based on his testimony, there is no evidence that the president -- the president of the Foca Assembly, Mladenovic, president of the Executive Committee of the Municipal Assembly of Foca, had in fact threatened him. In relation to the whole issue of the 1993 change of assignment, I just wish to refer the Chamber, the Appeals Chamber, to paragraph 2.42 -- rather, to our brief at large. An area of contention with regard to the nature of the lease agreement, the alleged lease agreement between, in fact, Krnojelac and also in fact the military command, I dare say in fact our position in regard to that lease agreement was that it didn't suffer from the strictures of any type of contractual arrangement but, more specifically, it was a case of a request being made by one body and a decision being made to accommodate that request. I think, in fact, I will refer to paragraph 2.42 of our brief where in fact mention is made of that agreement and our arguments again in relation to this particular area is in fact adequately mapped out in our brief. In addition, much has in fact been made with regard to the appellant's capacity to have effective control. And in paragraph 2.42, we make mention of paragraphs 46 and 47 of the Defence appeal brief where he alleged that from the 17th of April, 1992, until the formal conclusion of the agreement on the 10th of May, 1992, the military exercised factual power over the Muslim detainees in KP Dom, and members of the Uzice Battalion later replaced by members of the Livade company were in charge. The only evidence cited in these paragraphs of the Defence appeal brief is the testimony of Prosecution witness FWS-86, a detainee in the KP Dom, who said that the appellant allowed him to leave the KP Dom but with the permission of the Uzice Battalion that had to be secured. This testimony was, in fact, expressly referred to in the Trial Chamber and is entirely consistent with the Trial Chamber's findings that, and if I may quote, one important ramification of the lease agreement with the military was that it was the military command, and in particular Commander Kovac and not the Ministry of Justice who had the power to make decisions concerning which non-Serbs detainees would be detained in and released from KP Dom. And the Trial Chamber's finding that it was not satisfied that in his position as temporary warden and then warden the accused could unilaterally order or grant the release of any detainee, which is in fact consistent with the evidence. Further, as the Trial Chamber further noted, a warden does not generally have a unilateral power of release and at the KP Dom it was the Ministry of Justice who had the power over the continued detention of convicted Serb detainees and then the accused. They also recognised additionally that in fact the military command also in fact had some kind of sway over in fact non-Serb detainees. It wasn't a case, for example, where they were putting all power and responsibility in the hands of Krnojelac. Specific mention is made also of an incident involving Dzevad Lojo to the extent that while he was in fact being interviewed by Krnojelac, a guard came in and interrupted the interview to the extent indicating that in fact, listen, you are taking too much time with this man; finish it. What is significant, and we make mention of this in our brief at 2.44, is that -- is that no mention is made of the fact by my learned friend that that witness also testified that the appellant told this person to cease interrupting and to leave him and the witness alone. And this is to be found at T624, line 11, to T626, line 14. So in fact it is no indicator that there was some kind of incursions being made on the capacity of effective control displayed by Krnojelac in this incident. It was a case in fact -- in point where he displayed control, and he told the guard the position to the effect of, listen, don't interrupt me, full stop. I think it may be relevant at this point in time to deal also with the concept of de jure control, because it is the Prosecution's position, and it was in fact the Trial Chamber's position that the accused's de jure power derived from his power -- his position as warden of KP Dom. It is important to note though that that this is not the first time, for example, that questions have been raised with regard to de lege or de facto authority of a individual operating in an environment that is quite fluid. And this is why, for example, the Tribunal's jurisprudence has created a line of criteria we can consider in determining whether in fact the de jure control has in fact been in some way diverted by de facto control from another source. And these factors have in fact been mentioned in -- in various judgements. More specifically in the Kunarac judgement at paragraph 397 and paragraph 399 and the Kordic judgement at 418. And they indicated that factors relevant to the finding of effective control of a superior over de facto subordinates may include but are not limited to the capacity to sign orders, the substance of the orders and whether they are acted upon, formal procedures for appointment or office, the position of the accused in the overall institutional, political, and military organisation, the actual tasks performed such as the high public profile of the accused, his overall behaviour towards subordinates and his duties. In dealing with the whole question of high public profile, one may well consider and remember that in fact he did liaise on various occasions with the ICRC, the International Red Cross, with regard to detainees' imprisonment and in terms of the whole question of food. Apart from that, one would appreciate, for example, that in addition, the giving of orders, the exercise of powers generally attached to a military command, the submitting of reports to competent authorities in order to -- for proper measures to be taken, and sanction and power may also be considered. And I think it is an area that in fact we need to appreciate when we speak of sanction and power. The Aleksovski judgement speaks of that very sanction and power and has defined it in paragraph 78 as the possibility of transmitting reports to appropriate authorities suffices once a civilian authority through its position in the hierarchy is expected to report whenever crimes are committed and that in the light of this position, the likelihood that those reports will trigger investigation or disciplinary or criminal measures is extant. So that when one looks at the whole question of sanction and power, we need to be realistic in terms of how it operates. In the same way that a civil servant is able in fact to go to his line and also for example that does not prevent him from going to other line ministers in various ministries. And when you look at, for example, Krnojelac, he did write to the Defence Minister. He did write to the finance ministry. He did write to the War Presidency. So in fact he was quite aware, through his various memoranda in terms of the various requests that he made of them that therein lie the facility for communicating any type of complaints that he had. And in those circumstances, in the light of obviously all the beatings that were going on and being so informed about these beatings by various detainees, he was in a position to do likewise. He wanted food, so what did he do? He in fact sent a memo to, in fact, the Ministry of the Economy. He want the oil for the purposes of security. What did he do? He sent a letter, a memorandum asking for 20 tons of oil. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Schomburg would like to ask you a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: My apologies, but you're touching just upon a very serious question. I take it that it's the opinion of the Prosecution that it's immaterial whether or not the possible intervention or the attempt to intervene has any chance to be successful. So even if one would regard these ministers, in theory, as members of a joint criminal enterprise, being also responsible for the events there, and it would make no sense at all to alert them in writing because they know what's happening. What would be the sense of intervening by writing? Would it have the preventing effect foreseen under 7(3)? And second, how in the opinion of the Prosecution can a warden punish the persons you mentioned and mentioned in -- primarily in the indictment and in the pre-trial brief? So could I please hear your opinion on this serious question of how is it possible to prevent, and how is it possible to punish, and is it necessary that there is a likelihood or a strong chance that a person succeeds in doing so? If you would do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: Yes, yes. My lead counsel would respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution would submit that the answers to these questions lie in the very most fundamental purposes of international humanitarian law, which is to prevent these crimes from happening and to do so by making persons accountable. And that purpose would be defeated if loopholes were made available to allow people to escape accountability by saying, "I had nothing I could effectively do because everybody was in on the crime. Because everybody else was in on the crime that means that I'm not responsible for my part in it." We would submit that a commander has to have a mechanism for preventing or punishing. The mere fact that you are the commander means that you can give orders. If orders are disobeyed, that's another question. The power to punish, it has been held, may consist of no more than reporting to other authorities who can take the matter further, but we would submit the duty to report is always there. If the matter is reported and those to whom it is reported do nothing, the responsibility may lie there as well. And ultimately, and I believe there is case law at this Tribunal to that effect, if a commander is able to do nothing, the one thing that is always left to the commander is to remove himself or herself from that situation. A commander can always resign that position. It's a similar logic to saying that duress is no defence to crimes involving the taking of human life. If everybody simply refused to do it, if they refused to be a commander, these crimes could not happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. But wouldn't -- just this suggestion, and I know that your comments are based on a line of authorities, but to evade by just stating, "I leave my job because I can't stand any longer," would you regard this as a justification for not having reported and not having punished? Couldn't this be that you correctly mentioned a kind of evasion from responsibility?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would submit, no. It's a bit like asking: Is a commander relieved of responsibility if they had alarming information and yet undertook no inquiry because they felt the inquiry would turn nothing up, because they knew the perpetrators were so good at hiding things? There is -- it's speculative to ask what might have happened if the duty had been fulfilled. Even if the person to whom this matter is reported one believes will do nothing, it's impossible to know what might happen. It may be that outside organisations or NGOs would somehow find out about it and bring pressure to bear. But to simply say, "I can sit back and do nothing notwithstanding I have a legal obligation to do nothing because I deem that anything I tried to do would be ineffective, therefore, I don't even need to try," our submission is that is contrary to the very fundamental purpose of international humanitarian law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this additional explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: I'm much obliged. So that when one looks at the powers of in fact Krnojelac in his capacity as warden, we see certain things emanating. For example, Defence witnesses Milan Pavlovic and Miroslav Krsmanovic testify that they were transferred from the army units to the KP Dom due to the interventions by the accused and Misun Jokanovic. And this in fact relates to the Exhibit P3 which is attached -- which in fact is attached to the arguments as laid out by my learned friend. There were various documents signed by the warden that illustrate in fact his position of authority. Apart from various documents where in fact he actually had the stamp of Acting Warden, Temporary Warden, there were also situations where, in his requests for landmines, which in fact is Exhibit P445, the accused complained that the number of guards were inadequate to guard the prison population of 488, which included 470 Muslim detainees, 10 Serb detainees, and 8 convicted persons from before the war. And the reason stated in request was that there was information of an attempt to escape, and it is confirmed by the Prosecution witness FWS-172, which stated -- who stated that in the morning of June 1992, Mitar Rasevic told detainees that he believed that an escape was being planned. And, of course, this wasn't the first time that the appellant in fact had been making a request. So you see a meeting of the minds, an ad idem, because one would see a relationship between Rasevic indicating very categorically that, listen, I am aware of escape plans. And in the same vein you hear about requests being made for additional landmines for the purpose of pre-empting such attempts. When one looks at in fact the Exhibit D39, a document in fact raised by my learned friend as a contentious one with regard to a request made by a letter written by, in fact, Krnojelac in relation to relocating the prison from Bilece to Foca. What in fact this document indicates, though, is that he stated that in order to implement the order of the Hercegovina Corps commander and transfer the detainees, the security should be improved. So what in fact was happening is he was in fact requesting more security in the KP Dom. When one looks further at P446, another exhibit, it further shows the scope of the accused's de jure power over the whole of the KP Dom. The document prepared by Savo Todovic and signed by the accused on the 23rd of November, 1992 as warden, concerns lists of men liable for military service, members of the Foca KPD unit, and refers to 50 names of which the accused appears as name number one with the rank of captain first class. Savo Todovic and Mitar Rasevic in fact appear as names number two and three respectively. And what is significant is that on that particular list, all the men on that list except the accused are listed as soldiers, yet he's captain. And the point made by the Prosecution and accepted, in the compound he had the highest military rank among the staff at the KP Dom. The record is replete with evidence of, in fact, Krnojelac's integral role in the entire system. Many witnesses spoke about the way he dressed, the way in fact he carried himself. They spoke about in fact that he took part in a drill with a backpack in what appeared to be an alert for a drill. And this is to be found in FWS-69's statement, T4130 to 4131. Apart from that, even in relation to the incident involving FWS-86 where, in fact, FWS-86 was speaking specifically in relation to an argument that arose as a result of the intervention of in fact Krnojelac when attempts were made by the Uzice Corps to remove two detainees from the camp. And it is significant to read exactly -- to state what in fact he said. He said, for example, FWS-86, at T1469 to 1473, that during the said meeting - in other words, the accused -- FWS observed a heated argument between the accused and a commander from the Uzice Corps involving the removal of two detainees. The accused said, "I am responsible here inside the KP Dom" and refused to let anyone take out detainees unless he received a written confirmation giving full signatures and full names. Apart from that, he gave authorisation for FWS-86 to leave KP Dom to check on his elderly uncle although he had to do so with the acquiescence of the commander of the Uzice Corps. He was the one responsible for hiring his son as his bodyguard in the camp. So when in fact you look at the role of in fact the appellant, it is patent that in fact he did display not only de jure -- did display well de jure powers with regard to how in fact the camp operated, specifically in the area of release. I wish to refer the Court to Exhibit D67, Ekrem Zekovic, T3606, release 6th of October 1994, where on the 15th of May, 1992, the accused filed a request for the release of Enes Zekovic to the Foca Crisis Staff. And on the 13th of July, 1992, he notified the Foca Tactical Group of request for release of Ismet Pasovic and Sadik Demirovic. He also had a telephone number of the Crisis Staff and gave it to Fikret Abdic in relation to securing the release of RJ. So that even when one goes further and looks at the whole issue with regard to the beatings, more particularly concerning the attempted escape of Ekrem Zekovic, much has been said that Ekrem Zekovic incident comes at the end of his tenure, that in fact it took place on the 9th of July, some three weeks before he left the camp. But I must remind this Honourable Chamber that this particular incident, in fact, came subsequent to he being informed of two suspicious deaths in the camp - the death of Dzamilija, the death of Konjo - and you're talking about in fact a particular factual matter that is in fact on a higher plane than one simply being beating. You're talking about two suspicious deaths. So that even as far as back as 1992, notwithstanding in fact he's leaving when the Ekrem Zekovic matter in fact is experienced by him, even then he would have been put on effective notice and he would have had the responsibility, based on inquiry notice and based on actual knowledge with regard to beatings that of course RJ mentioned to him, to do the needful. Another piece of startling information in terms of the capacity that lied therein to arrest the situation. When, for example, the new warden came on, that is Zoran Sekulovic, at the end of July 1992, FWS-182 testified that conditions got drastically better. He testified that the attitude of the guards changed significantly when the accused was no longer the warden of KP Dom. The witness described the guards as much softer. So that one obviously recognises that that particular residual power, if you may describe it as that, that was there all the time was simply exercisable by in fact the new warden. Apart from that, there is -- there is again evidence in the record that the accused admits that he had morning meetings on a daily basis with heads of the business section. Detainees would see him walking around KP Dom and in his office with Mitar Rasevic and Savo Todovic. Witness FWS-250 saw the accused having breakfast regularly at the canteen with Savo Todovic and Mitar Rasevic. Now, these may in fact appear to be evidence simpliciter, and in those circumstances one would anticipate that it's quite reasonable that a Trial Chamber wouldn't mention all these little facets of evidence, but at the end of the day, on the totality of the evidence, on the cumulative evidence, they came to the conclusion that in fact that he was responsible under 7(3). Again, I have mentioned in my initial arguments yesterday in relation to the conduct of Burilo who in fact had a notorious reputation before the camp, during the camp, which notorious reputation was acted out in front of the appellant. Yet the appellant in fact -- there is no indication that he made any report considering that matter. And this whole question about retroactive investigation, does it mean for example that because a commander in fact hears about an incident three weeks before he leaves that in fact he is, in fact, in no way responsible or he is in no way put on inquiry notice to do the wherewithal. The bottom line is in relation to Krnojelac, there was a very definitive area that in fact he could have addressed directly or indirectly. He in fact had the position of the de jure prison warden. He specifically in fact dichotomised his responsibility in the context of director of the Drina Economic Unit and prison warden. To the extent that he did so he was quite aware that there were two areas of responsibility. And the thing -- the bottom line is that in fact the Trial Chamber recognised that he didn't have all-encompassing power over all the guards because they recognised it in the judgement. They mentioned it. But at the bottom line is at the end of the day in fact there was more than sufficient information for him to be put on inquiry, to do the needful, which in fact was not done. When one looks at the plethora of evidence in relation to beatings, the chain of information that came his way from RJ, from FWS-183, FWS-186, from FWS-66, various witnesses who in fact felt the brunt of in fact the system, and he did absolutely nothing. The Trial Chamber, in fact, found that he kept his head in the sand. But what the evidence illustrates here very categorically is that he was no ostrich, that in fact he had powers, powers in fact which were exercisable. He had lines of authority to which he in fact he could have addressed complaints, which he didn't. And more significantly, as a superior, he was responsible for his subordinates, guards who, for example, were both common in the Drina Economic Unit and also in fact in the military section. When one considers, for example, before I complete, I just wish to indicate, for example, that the accused himself confirmed that he provided the internal rules to the Ministry of Justice at a meeting when such rules were requested. So that in fact he in fact invoked rules previously in fact -- previously there to be part and parcel of in fact the system then. And what in fact it tends to show is to support the continuity between the organisation of the KP Dom before and during the war. In passing, I should add that there were many instances, two in particular where in fact Savo Todovic had to in fact get his signature to send documents on to higher authority. So that there was in fact subsisting this hierarchical relationship and this provided the mechanism for control which regrettably in fact was never invoked. Without more, this essentially, in fact, are the submissions. I wish to indicate that we are also adopting in toto our arguments in the brief as it relates to the particular areas of concern. And if in fact the learned Tribunal -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Carmona, you referred to the powers and assignments of the accused as the KP Dom warden. Particularly, you refer to the powers and assignments that he had or residual powers that he might have had and those powers -- residual powers he might have exercised. Relating of course to the non-Serbs and the Muslims, could you tell us, what were his powers? What were his authorities that he did have and that he didn't use for reasons that were well-founded or not well-founded? Could you give us some information on that point? Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: Well, in relation to -- in relation to his powers, he was a repository of perennial complaints from various prisoners. When one considers, for example, how prisoners came to make complaints to him, they would first in fact have to report it to a guard who would bring them -- bring that particular individual to the office, who subsequently in fact would bring that individual into his office. As much as in fact for example he said in fact he couldn't do much, there were many instances where in fact, for example, attempts were made by him to in fact do certain things with regard to food rations. Apart from that, there were certain specific guards who in fact belonged both to the Drina Economic Unit and belonged in fact to guards who also in fact were in charge of the non-Serbs. And this was by an admission by him in evidence. To the extent that these guards -- he was -- he was the warden, he would have in fact been in charge of those individuals. Apart from that, some of the guards who were there were formerly guards in KP Dom who were brought back by virtue of a decree into work assignments. So, apart from the fact that these particular individuals belonged to -- belonged to the regime before and were there still is an indication in fact that he did have control. And when one considers that a directive came to him to be in charge of the internal conditions of the place coupled with the fact that when guards attempted to remove detainees he was quite adamant, as I mentioned just a moment ago that he ought not to be removed without the proper accreditation, if I may so describe it, all of this is an indicator that he in fact did have control over these guards. And if I may refer also to paragraphs 105 to 106 in the judgement and paragraph 103 also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Carmona, could you give us one or two examples which would show that the accused was unable to make use of his powers and responsibilities and the constraints that he experienced afterwards following the division of the KP Dom into military and civilian sections?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: When one -- when one looks at the evidence in relation to RJ, who in fact the Court relied on tremendously, RJ in fact had made various complaints to him with regard to beatings that were going on, beatings that he in fact would have been quite aware of by virtue of where in fact his office was. Apart from that when one looks at in fact the Defence Exhibit 29 Official Gazette order which spoke of the internal runnings of the particular prison, mention is made particularly of the fact that apart from the workers employed at that institution being there that they would have gotten the assistance of in fact the employees of the Ministry of Interior police and MUP, so that as much as in fact he may have in fact been in a position of some -- of some doubt at times, he very well knew that there were in fact mechanisms which enabled prison authorities to deal with situations like that. Because you will remember, when he was confronted with the death of Konjo by the nurse and the nurse mentioned for example that an investigation committee had come in to deal with the situation he accepted it and didn't pursue it. So obviously he was aware that there were indeed mechanisms in the system to deal with situations of abuse. FWS-138, a guard who worked before and during that incident, before the camp and who in fact was a detainee, spoke of in fact lines of communication between the various organisations that were still subsistent even during the said conflict. Albeit not identical, but certainly there. Even further, that really there was no division. There was one structure. When you look at, for example, how in fact -- when people were injured, how they were fed together albeit at various times, how they were housed together, albeit in different rooms, they were essentially one structure. The only limitation, though, with regard to Krnojelac, however, was in the area of release. And in any -- in any ordinary organisation, whether in fact it is one that is democratically run or situations like that, very often a prison warden doesn't really have powers of release. He has powers of recommendation, as in fact was done in this particular case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Schomburg.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. A fundamental question which goes in both directions and covers both appeals, and it might serve maybe as a kind of judicial hint. The question for me, and please assist me with this, is the following: We are now in the situation, and you impressively discussed the question and described the superior responsibility, but we are faced with the situation that the Prosecution has pleaded in the first instance 7(1), 7(3) responsibility. In the second instance we have some acquittals and we -- some convictions are contested by the Defence, and in both situations, the Prosecution is pleading now merely 7(3) responsibility. My procedural question is: What is your opinion? Would it be for the Appeals Chamber? Would there be a possibility to come to the conclusion that in fact there is a 7(1) responsibility and a 7(3) responsibility or merely a 7(1) responsibility based on the fact that you are now pleading merely 7(3)?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: Yes. I think in fact -- this is a question that my lead counsel will respond to since in fact he has dealt with it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I clarify if I've correctly understood the question. Is the question that if 7(1) and 7(3) were both charged and the Trial Chamber acquitted on both and the Prosecution is now only appealing on 7(3) but that the Appeals Chamber thought that the correct characterisation of the facts when the law is correctly applied to them would be Article 7(1) responsibility, whether the Appeals Chamber would have a discretion to make such a finding notwithstanding that this was not expressly the ground of appeal? Your Honour, if that is the express question, I have to concede that I've not come to court prepared to argue that, and if that is an important question, I would request leave to file something in writing on it. And perhaps the Defence would want an opportunity to respond to that since I suspect that my colleague for the Defence may also not have come to court today prepared to argue that question, which is an important one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, and, therefore, I emphasise it's a question directed to both parties because the same to a certain extent might be a question. I don't know whether at the end of the day in fact it will be a question, but also in cases where, for example, the Defence is contesting now the judgement of first instance and primarily you are relying now on the 7(3) responsibility even though the pleading in the first instance in the indictment was a 7(1) and a 7(3) responsibility. So the question goes in both directions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: As I say, Your Honour, I think if that were a question that arose at this stage, the appropriate course would be to take it on notice and to submit something in writing. The Prosecution, as I say, hasn't come prepared to argue this, but even if I were to take it extemporaneously, I'm not sure that my colleagues of the Defence would be prepared to argue it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. We might probably come back to this later. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your microphone, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: It is now my esteemed pleasure to introduce my colleague Ms. Rashid who in fact will be dealing with the second ground of appeal, individual responsibility for persecution, imprisonment and living conditions, rather in terms of the response -- sorry. The response. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RASHID
utterances.text: May it please the Court. Your Honour, I will be responding to the appellant's second ground of appeal. I don't plan to respond to all the arguments that he has raised simply because most of the arguments have been adequately, comprehensively responded to in the Prosecution response brief. I will take about five minutes, though, to respond very briefly to one of the legal errors that learned counsel has raised, and that relates to the mens rea of an aider and abettor for the crime of persecution. Your Honour, the appellant has argued that in order for the appellant to be liable as an aider and abettor for the crime of persecution, the aider and abettor must share the same discriminatory intent of the perpetrator committing the crime of persecution. The Trial Chamber in the judgement in this case has held that as a matter of law, to find the appellant guilty of aiding and abetting the persecution of the non-Serb detainees, the Prosecution had to establish that the appellant had knowledge that the principal offenders intended to commit the underlying crimes constituting persecution, and that by their acts they intended to discriminate against the non-Serb detainees and that, with that knowledge, he made a substantial contribution to the commission of the discriminatory acts committed by the principal offenders. The Prosecution agrees with the Trial Chamber's legal finding. In his argument, the Prosecution notes that he has not referred to a single authority except he cited today the Kupreskic Trial Chamber or Appeals Chamber's judgement - I'm not clear on that one - in support of his proposition. The accused -- sorry, Your Honour. The appellant's assertion is in any case unsupported by the prevailing Tribunal jurisprudence. The appellant has essentially considered that for all other crimes apart from persecution, the aider and abettor need not share the requisite mens rea. No reasons have been offered, either in his appeal brief or at today's hearing, as to why the crime of persecution should be treated any differently in the context of individual responsibility. Your Honour, we have referred to the -- all the relevant cases that we could find in our response brief supporting our submissions that there is clear jurisprudence both at trial and at the appeals level in support of the Trial Chamber's legal finding on the mens rea of an aider and abettor on the crime of persecution. More pertinently, I must point out that this issue has been resolved by the Appeals Chamber, by at least three Appeals Chambers, and no cogent reasons have been advanced as to why this Appeals Chamber should revisit the issue or reconsider its previous ruling. I need only refer Your Honour to the Aleksovski appeal judgement, which followed the Furundzija appeal judgement at paragraph 162. I must point out the Kvocka trial judgement, which has acknowledged that the requisite mens rea of an aider and abettor of persecution as a special intent crime is broader. In the context of persecution, it was held that the aider and abettor of persecution must not only have knowledge of the crime that he's assisting or facilitating, but he must also be aware of the -- that the crimes were being committed -- sorry, with a discriminatory intent. So he must be aware of all the elements of the crime. He does not have to share this intent. All he needs to do is that he must be aware of the broader discriminatory contacts and know that his acts of assistance or encouragement have a significant effect on the commission of the crimes. The Kvocka Trial Chamber highlighted the importance of drawing a distinction between the mens rea of an aider and abettor and a co-perpetrator. It says that there is no need for a shared intent because if intent was shared this might elevate a secondary, that is an accomplice or an aider and abettor to the status of a co-perpetrator and this might dilute the distinction that the Appeals Chamber in Tadic has set out between participating in a joint criminal enterprise and aiding and abetting. So it is important to maintain that distinction. Now, learned counsel has today referred to the Kupreskic appeal judgement or trial judgement in support of his assertion. The only relevant finding that we could find referring to the elements for aiding and abetting is the one set out in the Kupreskic Trial Chamber's legal findings on this issue which was cited by the Appeals Chamber in its judgement. That's at paragraph 254, and it is in fact set out in our response brief in support of the Prosecution's argument. In fact, the Appeals Chamber adopted the Trial Chamber's finding that for an aider and abettor, he must only know that the acts performed by him assisted the commission of the persecutory act by others. So it doesn't support the Defence assertion at all. That is my submission, Your Honour. The rest of the arguments raised by the Defence has been adequately responded to. If I could be of any assist -- assistance I would be more than happy to do so. Then it is for me to introduce my colleague Ms. Helen Brady and she will be addressing the Court on the fourth and the fifth grounds of the appeal raised by the appellant. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. That introduction was a more lengthy one than I will probably be in my response, because indeed on grounds four and five which concern his Article 7(3) responsibility for beatings, both as inhumane acts and cruel treatment and persecutory beatings, most of these issues have already been dealt with in a very substantial way by my colleague Mr. Carmona this morning as well as we've extensively addressed these in our submissions yesterday when we were speaking of superior responsibility for torture. Clearly, there is an overlapping of issues here with the earlier issues relating to the first ground of appeal in particular. Today, Mr. Bakrac has mentioned two issues common to both grounds. The first is in relation to his knowledge about the beatings. All I need to say, I think, on that is that we have responded in great detail to the points raised in chapter 6 of our response brief, and we've also made a lot of submissions on this yesterday when I spoke on both the -- in the submissions on appeal and also in our reply. So I won't elaborate on those submissions. I think everything I have said on the subject needs to be said there. The other issue he referred to in relation to these two grounds is really that he was not a superior to the guards and so he can't bear 7(3) responsibility. And again, Mr. Carmona has extensively addressed this ground concerning his effective authority for 7(3) and shown that the Trial Chamber has made no error by concluding that Krnojelac was in this hierarchical relationship with the guards. And not only was he a de jure or legal superior, but he also had real powers over them sufficient for having a real or material ability to take steps to prevent or punish. There's nothing I need add to this except just to re-emphasise the need to take, just as the Trial Chamber did on this issue, and setting out its findings in ten very extensive pages with extensive footnotes citing the evidence that one needs to take a holistic approach to the evidence. In particular, paragraphs 102 to 103 and 318 of the judgement. And this analysis is certainly -- one cannot say, it is not one that no reasonable Trial Chamber could in fact have made. And in fact, I would just make one more point on this, and that's that the Trial Chamber's rigour in applying the test for effective control can be seen when it deals with the situation of the other people who were beating the detainees, those who were coming in, the military police, the interrogators, those who were coming in from outside. And there you will recall that the Trial Chamber found he wasn't in this hierarchical relationship, so he didn't bear 7(3) responsibility for their actions, only in relation to the actions of the guards and the actions of the guards in allowing them, permitting them into the camp and participating with them in those crimes. And I think that shows a rigour and certainty of analysis. Your Honours, that's all I'll say. All other aspects raised in his appeal brief are responded to in our written submissions in chapters 5 and 6 of the Prosecution response brief. If there are any questions, otherwise, I will be happy to introduce the final speaker, the senior appeals counsel Mr. Staker who will be addressing on sentence and concluding remarks. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: May it please the Chamber. The sentencing appeal can be dealt with very briefly. The standard of review in an appeal against sentence has been addressed in paragraph 9.2 of the Prosecution appeal brief and paragraph 11 of the Prosecution response brief. The case law on this is well known. The sentencing appeal is not a de novo hearing. It is not an opportunity for the party to rehearse the sentencing arguments that were presented before the Trial Chamber. What is necessary is to show that the Trial Chamber went outside its quite considerable discretion in matters of sentencing, that the error in sentencing was discernible, discernible being the test word used in the case law generally, or that there was an error of law in that the Trial Chamber took into account a matter which it was legally not entitled to take into account or that it refused to consider a matter that it was legally obliged to consider. In our submission, everything said by my colleague for the Defence today in the sentencing appeal has already been said in the Defence appeal brief and has already been responded to in the Prosecution response brief. The Prosecution's submission is at the end of the day the various matters referred to by my colleague for the Defence were all taken into account by the Trial Chamber in one way or another. It hasn't been shown that there has been a discernible error in sentencing or that the sentencing discretion has been exceeded. And indeed, if I understand my colleague for the Defence, this was in fact conceded by him if the transcript reflects correctly what was said, it says that the Defence does not think that the trial fully went beyond its discretionary right but that he wanted to raise certain sentencing factors in any event. Our submission is that that nonetheless does not satisfy the test for an appeal against sentence in this jurisdiction. The one matter that was raised which I believe is new was the argument that it may make a difference whether a number of crimes were committed within a short space of time or a long space of time. That's a matter I don't intend to go into. I think that's a matter that might be looked at either way by a Trial Chamber. I don't think there's any doubt that in this case the Trial Chamber was aware of the period in question and that it was aware of the scale of the crimes that were committed, and there's no suggestion that it didn't give it appropriate consideration in one way or the other. That -- with that, I conclude my submissions on the sentencing appeal. I would just proceed then to make a few concluding comments before ending the Prosecution submissions in response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Staker, excuse me. I want to ask you a question. When you talk about sentence, do you believe that your position in respect of asking for review upwards, in respect of whether the -- at the state -- status of the case when you began the appeal and the point where this discussion began, at some point in your office did you consider the sentence in respect of all the different sentences that have been pronounced at this Tribunal? There have been several, quite a few. Some were more spectacular than others. I would like to know what is the position of the OTP in respect of sentences. Did you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: I believe I've understood your question, Your Honour. I think the established law is that every sentence has to be individualised and that sentences imposed in other cases are a matter that can be looked at, bearing in mind, however, that each case has its own unique features. It's not possible to say that we have in this case a camp commander, therefore, the starting point is so many years, or that this person is convicted of three murders, therefore, the starting point is another case that involved a person who was convicted of three murders. In almost every case before this Tribunal, accused will be charged on multiple counts for acts that may be categorised as various different kinds of crimes, convicted on some, acquitted on others on different bases, whether it's superior responsibility, direct responsibility, aiding and abetting, and the personal circumstances will always vary considerably. So the starting point is not to draw strict comparisons with sentence imposed on other particular accused in other particular circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Shahabuddeen. Thank you, Mr. Staker.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Staker, it used to be the position in one jurisdiction that I know of that the Court is not overly concerned with previous cases and previous sentences passed in those cases, but I think the view has changed latterly in the opposite direction, that, well, the courts must respond to the public conscience, and the public conscience does not sit too easily with glaring discrepancies in sentencing and is not too easily appeased by intellectualised arguments as to the peculiar circumstances of one case having to be individualised and so on. There is, therefore, a movement in the direction, as I perceive it, of establishing some kind of tariff. I think this is what the President had in mind. We bear in mind very much what you have wisely said about the need for individualising sentences and taking the circumstances of each case into consideration, but at the end of the day, is there a movement now in response to an appreciation of the dictates of the public conscience to establish a kind of tariff.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the answer to that question, I think, is that any kind of tariff in a national system would normally be provided by a legislature. If in the Tribunal we do not have a legislature that could do that, it would be provided by the judiciary. And I do recall that in earlier sentencing appeals, if I remember correctly, the Prosecution did make a submission that gross discrepancies in sentencing would be a matter of concern, noted that in a national system normally some guidance is given for a start from the fact that most different kinds of crimes have different maximum sentences. Murder has a different maximum sentence under international law and every other system than grievous bodily harm or theft, whereas in the legal system of the Tribunal, every crime has a maximum sentence of life imprisonment. My recollection is that decision in the case in which this submission was made was nonetheless that in this legal system, every sentence is individualised and yet the Appeals Chamber at that stage considered it inappropriate to provide more detailed guidelines. It may be that that is a question that could be reopened. I would submit merely that the submission I've just made is one that follows the existing case law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there are no other questions, you can complete your comments, Mr. Staker.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. My concluding comment is just this: That the Defence appeal in this case is based largely on alleged errors of fact and that the standard of review in an appeal alleging errors of fact is well settled in the case law of the Tribunal. Members of the Bench have referred to it in the course of this appeal, and it's been addressed in the Prosecution response brief in Chapter 1. And the point that I would wish to emphasise in concluding is that the applicable test in an appeal alleging errors of fact is whether the decision of the Trial Chamber is one which no reasonable trier of fact could have come to on the evidence before it. And the situation is that for every finding of fact made in the trial judgement, there was evidence. In this case, there was a lot of evidence. There was a lot of evidence referred to in the trial judgement, and there was no doubt much evidence that was before the Trial Chamber that was not expressly referred to in the trial judgement. Now, I notice the Defence approach in this appeal is to refer to and to rely on the evidence that is inconsistent with the findings of the trial judgement, and we submit that that is not the correct approach. In any case before this Tribunal where there is large amounts of evidence, there will always be conflicting evidence. I doubt that any judgement is ever given -- it's probably the case in national courts as well: A judgement will not be given that is 100 per cent consistent with every item of evidence that was before the Court. The Court has to weigh conflicting evidence and come to its own conclusion. So simply pointing to evidence that is inconsistent with what the Trial Chamber found is not sufficient to establish that no reasonable trier of fact could have come to that conclusion. Indeed, we would submit that in an appeal alleging an error of fact, the focus is not on the evidence that was inconsistent with the Trial Chamber's findings, the focus must be on the evidence that supported the Trial Chamber's findings. One has to look at the evidence that the Trial Chamber relied upon in reaching its decision. And an error of fact may be established if it's found that there was no evidence at all for the conclusion it reached or if it's found that the evidence that the Trial Chamber relied on was such that no reasonable Trial Chamber could have accepted it as credible, or relied upon it, or if it's shown that no reasonable Trial Chamber could have drawn the inference of fact from that evidence that the Trial Chamber did, or that the evidence that it relied upon, when looked at together with other evidence in the case, cumulatively is not such that any reasonable Trial Chamber could have concluded that the conclusion was established beyond a reason doubt. Now, in our submission there is a danger that if, in an appeal alleging error of fact, there is a concentration on the inconsistent evidence, what we descend into is a new trial. It's not the responsibility of a respondent to go through all of the evidence that supported the Trial Chamber's findings and to explain why they support the findings the Trial Chamber reached, and I fear this hearing may have veered off in that direction slightly. We submit it's not for the Prosecution to explain why the Trial Chamber's findings are justified. The question is whether it has been proven, and the burden lies on the Defence that no reasonable trier of fact could have reached this conclusion based on the evidence before it. And we submit that if that is not established, the findings of the Trial Chamber stand. And I mean the findings of the Trial Chamber, because there's also the danger that there may be a suggestion that by reopening things, one's seeking to go beyond the Trial Chamber's findings and to make new or additional findings. That's not the case either. And the Prosecution position is that, apart from those specific areas of the trial judgement that we have appealed in our appeal, we submit that the finding, the judgement of the Trial Chamber stands unless and until it's shown that there is something in that so unreasonable that no reasonable trier of fact could have reached that conclusion, and our submission is that that has not been established by the appellant in this case. And unless I can be of further assistance, they are the submissions of the Prosecution in response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Shahabuddeen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Staker, I was interested in your peroration, from which I derive great assistance, but tell me, have I got it right? Your position is that in determining the issue whether any reasonable Tribunal of fact would have come to the conclusion reached by the Trial Chamber in question, regard is only to be had to the evidence which the Trial Chamber relied on for its findings? Is that perhaps too severe a view to take? Might there not be a case - Mr. Bakrac referred to it - in which there is some evidence which the Trial Chamber did not rely on for its findings but which a reasonable Tribunal of fact, if it took account of it, might say to itself that it couldn't come to the conclusion reached by the Trial Chamber on the facts which supported its findings?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry if I wasn't entirely clear in the submission I was making. Of course the evidence that one can look at in an appeal alleging error of fact is all of the evidence that was before the Trial Chamber. Of course one can't look at other evidence that was not before the Trial Chamber, subject only to Rule 115. But my submission is that when looking at whether there's been an error of fact, the starting point is to look at the evidence that the Trial Chamber did rely on and then -- and then perhaps proceed to say, in light of the inconsistent evidence, no reasonable trier of fact could have concluded on that evidence that it was proved beyond a reasonable doubt. But you can't ignore the evidence the Trial Chamber did rely on and only look at the inconsistent evidence, which is the approach, in our submission, the Defence has taken in this appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: That seems to me to be a slightly different position.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: I apologise if I wasn't clear. My point is to say that the starting point of the analysis is what the Trial Chamber did rely on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just to clarify this in my mind mainly. I think there are two points in issue at this point. One which has been raised by my colleague Judge Shahabuddeen, the other one which was raised by you. Do I take it that what Judge Shahabuddeen actually raised is a matter that belongs to us when we come to deliberate on on the appeal or that particular section of the appeal. The other one also belongs to us but refers particularly to the onus that you have in fulfilling your task as Prosecution defending or responding to the appeal of the Defence.
