In other words, what -- the point that you have made, and if I misread you, please do tell me so, is that it is not your job, your task in response to the appeal of the Defence, this particular appeal to show how or why the decision of the Trial Chamber as regards the evaluation of the fact ought to stand but, rather, it is the onus of the Defence to prove that there has been indeed been an error of fact. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: That's our position. In this case the Defence is appealing and the Prosecution is responding, but the position would be identical if the Prosecution was appealing and the Defence responding. But the burden is always on the appellant to persuade the Appeals Chamber that the standard is met and the respondent does not need to justify --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could it be our duty in fulfilling this exercise to take into consideration not only what is specifically referred to in the judgement of the Trial Chamber but also the sum totality of the evidence, including evidence that Judge Shahabuddeen has referred to which a reasonable Trial Chamber would or should have taken into consideration.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Well, yes. But the point I would keep returning to is that the analysis is what the Trial Chamber found. Therefore, one doesn't -- I mean, one is only looking at the trial judgement as it were what are the findings that the Trial Chamber made. In determining whether those findings were reasonable or unreasonable in the sense that no reasonable trier of fact could have reached them, the Appeals Chamber may look at the totality of the evidence in the case. But of course it's for the parties to identify the unreasonableness. As I said, the appellant bears the burden. If nothing is identified for the Appeals Chamber to find something proprio motu that the parties haven't had the opportunity of briefing or submitting argument on would be going beyond this contradictory adversary process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very interesting what you have just said for the Appeals Judges listening to you because you mentioned various points. And your criteria, trying to say that one should not look for whether or not there were contradictions of this piece of evidence because you think that when you look at all of the evidence that have been provided that there might be contradictions, that is something that would be of enormous interest to us, and we will take that into consideration. I think we've finished now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: One further clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: When I said that the Appeals Chamber can look at all the evidence in the case, the one clarification I make is that it can only look at the evidence that the Trial Chamber could have looked at and taken into account. The one situation that would cover is that if evidence were tendered but the Trial Chamber refused to admit it and therefore didn't take it into account, that couldn't be taken into account on appeal unless it had been established that the Trial Chamber was unreasonable in refusing to admit it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. That's a point that the Chamber is very familiar with. That's part of our own case law, but of course you're right to recall that. Judge Schomburg.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But isn't it true that this review of the evidence admitted at trial is limited to that extent that the appealing party has no doubt the onus to prevent -- present the flaws, and would it be not for the Appeals Chamber to go into a search exercise throughout all the admitted evidence in order to find out whether or not the Trial Chamber erred, for example, by not taking into account the one or other evidence? In conclusion, this would mean that the work of the Appeals Chamber would be limited to that end and to those alleged errors in coming to the facts of the case they adduced and submitted during the appeal. Would this be your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Essentially, yes, Your Honour. In any legal system, the judiciary plays a certain role. The appellant plays a certain role. The respondent plays a certain role. Others play a certain role. And that role is different in different legal systems. But in the legal system of this Tribunal, it's a -- well, a contradictory proceeding whereby a party invokes the judicial mechanism so that, for instance, I think it must be uncontroversial that the Appeals Chamber could not reverse a trial judgement on appeal if neither of the parties appealed. It's for the parties to invoke the appellate process, and it's for the parties to specify their ground of appeal. Therefore, the Appeals Chamber would not find errors in the judgement that have not been raised as any ground of appeal. I believe we have case law to that effect as well. The parties themselves are constrained in that they can't raise errors that are not included within their grounds of appeal unless they apply for and are given leave to amend those grounds. And it's part of the efficiency of the process that litigation doesn't become endless and uncontrollable and the mechanism for keeping procedures regular in this legal system is that the parties invoke the process and identify what they are seeking and this is ruled upon in due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. We're going to suspend, take a 20-minute break so that the Defence will have the final word in its reply. All right. At the request of the majority of Judges, Judge Shahabuddeen speaking for all, we will take a 30-minute break. And the Defence can prepare itself for the final reply and we'll give the last word to Mr. Krnojelac. Very well. We'll see one another again in 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will now resume the hearing. Have the accused brought in, please. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'd, with your leave, like to ask my co-counsel, Mr. Vasic, to give the reply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is your choice. Please go on, Mr. Vasic. Very well. We're listening.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Your Honours, learned friends, at this stage, in view of the exhaustive presentation of the grounds of both parties, the Defence will confine itself now to comments about some of the things that were said by my learned friend Mr. Carmona which, in the Defence's view, do not arise from the body of evidence available to the first instance Trial Chamber. To begin with, the Defence should like to clarify an issue which came up yesterday and today in the courtroom and had to do with the document dated 11th January 2000, which the Defence did not use during its case before the Trial Chamber. Why did not we -- why didn't we do that? Because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry. This is a document mentioned in paragraph 98? You're referring to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours. Let me just check it. Yes, that is the document. The reason we didn't do that is that the Trial Chamber -- because that is a document from the year 2000 and the Trial Chamber recommended to the Defence to think about it and to check the probative value of such a document, and the Defence then, as it had more evidence to produce dating to 1992 and 1993 about the same or even identical facts, the Defence, therefore, decided not to tender that particular document into evidence as its exhibit. So that was the reason insofar as that document is concerned. My learned friend Mr. Carmona, when referring to the position of the accused in the KP Dom, said that the fact that he was the warden and that the hierarchical structure in the KP Dom did not change, and he said that the witness FWS-138's testimony corroborated that position. That witness was a guard in the KP Dom prior to the conflict, and for a while he was also detained in the KP Dom. I think that our learned friends in the Prosecution themselves submitted during the case that -- that the detainees did not often leave the rooms that they were detained in, so the question arises how could they assess accurately the organisation of the prison's administration at the time when they were kept in it? On other hand, we heard in the course of the proceedings a large number of witnesses for the Prosecution who said that Milorad Krnojelac was a paper warden or a de jure warden which could also fit into their subjective appreciation of the situation on the basis of what they could see, bearing in mind the position they were in. However, the Defence produced some other evidence to the same effect, showing that Milorad Krnojelac's role was completely different. Those were guards who worked in the KP Dom at the time relevant for the indictment and who stated that Milorad Krnojelac was not their superior, that he issued no orders to them, and that was also firsthand testimony. The third category of evidence produced to show the same point are documents which Milorad Krnojelac sent to his ministry, that is the Ministry of Justice, under whose jurisdiction he was and which clearly show what were his powers, what were his terms of reference. And we think that if one juxtaposes this evidence on the one hand and the FWS-38's statement on the other, then that the only conclusion we can arrive at is that -- what immediate participants, that is guards, present should -- and documents which Milorad Krnojelac wrote at the critical period should be given more weight. My learned friend also said that it was the duty of a warden to report to the Ministry of Justice about beatings that were happening at the relevant period, again on the basis of the testimony of the above-mentioned witness FWS-138. It is indisputable that in peacetime any such violent act means an infraction of the rules of service and needs to be reported to the Ministry of Justice. However, bearing in mind the situation in Foca in 1992/1993 when the KP Dom had been leased to the army so that it could keep the non-Serb population there, the detained non-Serb population, it was quite clear that the Ministry of Justice had no jurisdiction over that wing of that part of the KP Dom and that it was under a completely different administration which could possibly communicate with the commander of the unit which supervised the prison. At the time when those ministries were put in place and when they were operational, bearing in mind at that time one could hardly go along with the conclusion about the fluid nature of those institutions according to which, I presume, the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Justice might be interwoven with that of the Ministry of Defence or some other ministry, and I think that if one does have a government in place, if one does have -- if one has ministries in place, something like that would be impossible. The Defence, therefore, thinks that such a conclusion is untenable and that the Ministry of Justice had jurisdiction only over that part of the KP Dom in Foca where prisoners from before the conflict were kept and in that segment of the KP Dom which was called the Drina Economic Unit. Needless to say that different ministries communicate at the government level, and I think that that is the only reasonable level allowing us to conclude that the government is performing its -- the duties it is supposed to perform. My learned friend also mentioned the exhibit of the Prosecution, P2, to corroborate his submission that there was no division in the administration of individual parts of the KP Dom, and he based his conclusion on the fact that although the kitchen and the hospital had been leased to the Foca Tactical Group, they nevertheless were used by other prisoners too. If one -- if one looks carefully at a number of exhibits addressing the state of affairs in that part which was under Milorad Krnojelac's jurisdiction according to the Defence, and that is the Defence Exhibit 85, it's the document which is the report of Milorad Krnojelac that he's submitting to the Ministry of Justice, and if one looks at it carefully, then one can see that there were only six prisoners who for reasons that my colleague mentioned because who for -- were either alcoholics or drug addicts and who were, for that reason, put in the KP Dom. And it is only natural that there was no need to build a new kitchen or a new infirmary for six prisoners. Therefore, we do not think that the conclusion can be accepted that the Defence did not raise the question of these six prisoners earlier since their presence arises from Exhibit D85, which states it quite clearly. And it even indicates for each of these prisoners individually why he is being detained in the KP Dom. As for the allegations of my learned friend regarding the terms of reference, the mandate of Milorad Krnojelac as the warden and manager of the Drina Economic Unit, and he also mentioned Prosecution's Exhibit 3, the Defence thinks that it is precisely this exhibit which shows best the degree of changes made in the administration of the prison in relation to the peacetime setup, and in particular in that part of it. At the time when Milorad Krnojelac was responsible for the civilian part, we see that there was no other manager of the economic unit. And after the summer of 1993, we have this -- we see that this office reappears but then there is a manager in place, there are his assistants there too, which shows that during the critical period of time there were only 27 prisoners at the Drina Economic Unit which were the only part, the only aspects of the KP Dom that Milorad Krnojelac was responsible for. My learned friend mentioned also the mining of the KP Dom, submitting that it was done to prevent the escape of prisoners of war. The evidence presented and the statement of Milorad Krnojelac himself show that out of concern for the storage space that was in that -- that was located in that part of the KP Dom next to the wall which was not secured that he was present at the time when the military laid the mines and that it was not done because of the prisoners of war. And a similar thing could be said of the request to procure oil or petrol or the security system. So some of the oil was used in the production. And as for security system, it could only be used to supply the electric energy, that is the lighting, as the one who is leasing the KP Dom is bound to do. And I think that this request may not be interpreted as my learned colleague tried to do. I do not see how else could oil be used in the security system unless it was for lighting. As for the working hours and Milorad Krnojelac's presence in the KP Dom, I think that it is less important whether working hours were from 7.00 in the morning until 3.00 in the afternoon or until 4.00 in the afternoon. However, it is not true that it was only once when he went to visit his son who had lost both his legs that he was absent from the KP Dom on that one occasion only. In addition to the testimony of witnesses who worked at the Drina Economic Unit and who testified about daily duties that Milorad Krnojelac had to discharge which had to do with Foca and its surroundings and which also had to do with his efforts to restart the production at the Drina Economic Unit, the Defence also tendered into evidence a number of travel orders which show where and when Milorad Krnojelac travelled during the critical period. The next submission that the Defence should like to touch upon is -- is the fact that Milorad Krnojelac accepted the labour obligation fearing that he might be arrested for failing to do so. My learned friend challenges that and relies on Mr. Tesovic's and Mr. Cancar's case, who allegedly did not suffer any consequences for refusing to take up the post which was later on taken up by Milorad Krnojelac. The Defence finds it necessary to point out once again that Exhibit P3 shows clearly that Mr. Tesovic left Foca in the wake of the outbreak of the conflict, taking a number of prisoners to Tuzla. He had to pass through Montenegro, Serbia on his way and that he was absent until May 1992. And allow me to remind you that Mr. Milorad Krnojelac was appointed the temporary warden in the end of April. Therefore, nobody could appoint Mr. Tesovic to that post, nor even ask him if he wanted to, if he was ready to accept it. After his return to Foca, there was already a new warden. As for Mr. Cancar and the statement that he gave in the court in Sarajevo where he was the accused and when later he was released in spite of a very severe sentence, I believe that my co-counsel has already -- that my lead counsel has already addressed this question extensively and that will be a matter for the Appeals Chamber to decide upon. My learned friend also claimed that in point of fact, the army placed the authority in the hands of Milorad Krnojelac. But that conclusion is completely wrong. First of all because there is evidence about his appointment, documents which come from the Ministry of Justice to which he reports and to which he is accountable, and I do not think that there should be any dispute about that. And the relationship or, rather, the actual authority which Milorad Krnojelac might have in relation to the military and the guards which my learned friends insist upon, I think can best be gleaned from two instances that were mentioned today. One is the witness Dzevad Lojo, when the guard warned Milorad Krnojelac that the conversation was not permitted and that he did it repeatedly. That is a very important fact. And that after that, Milorad Krnojelac, as my colleague puts it, told him to stop interrupting him. It is difficult to imagine that a subordinate could behave in such a manner. Even more drastic is an example that has to do with Ekrem Zekovic, where according to the testimony of this witness, the guard Burilo, although Milorad Krnojelac was present snatched, that is pushed him, snatched Zekovic from him and then banged him against a call. One could hardly imagine such an attitude towards a warden who has factual power and authority. One could hardly imagine that a simple guard could treat him in this manner. But my learned friend submitted today that it has been established that Milorad Krnojelac was a superior of some guards but not of all of them. I think that it will be fair that a step forward been made -- had a further step forward been made to establish who were those guards who were subordinate to Milorad Krnojelac and which guards were not, so that we could see then whether those guards who were his subordinates did commit some crimes or was he a superior of those guards who had not committed any crimes. And would it be fair then to view his responsibility under 7(3) in that light.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Agius wants to ask a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I'm beginning to think or believe that you have not read paragraph 317 of the judgement which lists precisely the guards that, according to the Trial Chamber, were personally responsible for some of the atrocities, for the beatings that took place in the KP Dom, and these are precisely the guards that the Trial Chamber considers your client to have been responsible for. Paragraph 317, starting on page 126 and continuing on page 127.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I was only referring to what my learned colleague the Prosecutor stated here. He didn't mention what -- he didn't give the reference of what he had stated, so I thought that what I -- I thought that my comment was appropriate. In addition to what I have said, in paragraph 317 of the judgement, the Defence doesn't see on the basis of what arguments certain selection was made. Who are the guards who were not subordinates of Mr. Krnojelac? But as I said, this was just a response to what my learned colleague from the Prosecution had said since a reference had not been provided when this issue was raised. My learned colleague also mentioned the contact that the International Red Cross had with Milorad Krnojelac, and he considered that this -- these meetings had to do with the detainees and with improving the food. I don't think that there is any evidence that would point to the fact that there was contact with Milorad Krnojelac with regard to imprisoning individuals. There were meetings about food, and he explained -- the accused explained that he tried to improve the food and to obtain food for all those who were detained in the KPD. As far as the allegation -- as far as the allegations that demonstrate the effective power that Milorad Krnojelac had, the allegation that on the basis of his intervention the witnesses Pavlovic and Krsmanovic were enabled to visit the KPD, I think that this fact has been very well explained in the testimony of these witnesses, and I think that he asked these people from the military command to help him set the Drina Economic Unit -- to put it into function again. These people were demobilised and were provided him for assistance. And while they were his subordinates, they weren't mobilised into military units. As far as Exhibit D39 is concerned, that was mentioned by my learned colleague and relates to a report of Milorad Krnojelac with regard to transferring the Bilece prison to the KPD in Foca, we have to say that this report has to do with his report in which it is stated what is essential to be done in order to make such a transfer possible. A transfer is not implied in it, it isn't requested, it isn't ordered. This is just a report which says that if they want to make this transfer to the KPD in Foca, they have to ask the Ministry of Justice. First of all, they have to have a contract in order to lease certain premises and they have to provide the guards who will provide security for the detainees, just like the Foca Tactical Group provided security when it signed the contracts on leasing the KPD that we have been discussing here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suppose that -- well, you are speaking very slowly, much more slowly than the Prosecutor talks. So we have to be completely equal in the time distribution. We have to measure or take into account the speed of the speakers as well. You're speaking more slowly than your colleagues, but we do have to maintain balance, and I want to know whether you still have a great deal to say in your reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your understanding, Your Honour. I don't have -- I don't need a lot more time. Perhaps another ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, how many minutes do you -- all right. You have five minutes. We have to take a decision. You have got five more minutes. You should be able to summarise things, and I'm sure within five minutes you should be able to reply to the Prosecution, otherwise, we're going to have Mr. Staker get up and say, come on, I want to speak longer too. So make an effort, please, Mr. Vasic. Thank you very much. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I didn't notice that I had already gone over time. As far as the request that Milorad Krnojelac forwarded to the Crisis Staff and the fact that he had the telephone of the Crisis Staff, I don't think this can be taken to be proof that he was part of the hierarchy that my learned colleagues had been referring to. The Defence has explained why he forwarded these requests. The reason for this was that he wanted to help people, but this wasn't part of his responsibilities. He wasn't responsible for those detainees, and the telephone number of the Crisis Staff or going to the -- going to the canteen for lunch with Rasevic, I don't think that if this is taken into consideration with all the other evidence, I don't think that this is proof that he was part of that hierarchy. As far as the claim that there were guards is concerned, that there were guards who worked both in the KPD and in the Drina Economic Unit, I think that this has been explained and that when the guards worked in the Drina Economic Unit, they weren't mobilised into the army. The people who worked there were civilians, but when they worked as guards, that was after the mobilisation, and they were responsible, they answered to the military authorities. So those would be all my comments in response to the Prosecution's allegations apart from the fact that in the written brief, in the written response to the Prosecution's appeal, in item 3 and 4, my learned colleagues suggest under the ground of appeal number 2 -- ground of appeal number 2, that if -- that the only legal remedy that could be acceptable would be to revise the Trial Chamber's judgement, and they suggest that the existing sentence should be changed under count 1 and there should be -- they should take into account count 11. This has to do with the crime of persecution on the basis of imprisonment. The Defence considers that in the judgement delivered by the Trial Chamber, it is stated that Milorad Krnojelac was acquitted on count 11 and that this decision of the Trial Chamber with regard to count 11 was not the subject of an appeal by the Prosecution. So such a revision would not be permissible, and that would be tampering with the fairness of the decision. If you have no other questions, the Defence has finished, has concluded its remarks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Vasic. This is the end of the hearing. You may be seated. We've reached the end of the hearing. The Chamber, according to the principles and standards of international law, we, as the last point, must listen to what Mr. Milorad Krnojelac would like to say to us if he would like to stand. Perhaps he should come to the front. He could come with his guard and stand in front of us. Madam Registrar, would you please organise this. If you like, Mr. Krnojelac, you can come over here, up in the front. Come up here in front of us. We'll ask the usher to help you settle in. Thank you. You may be seated if you like. If not, just proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm a little surprised. I have been following this hearing, these appellate proceedings for two days now, but since you have allowed me to address you, there is not much that I want to say because I think that a lot has been said already, and I'm not capable of speaking about matters that I am not prepared for and that I haven't studied for because, as I can see, these are all legal matters. I work in the field of education. So I would like to say a few words, but if I go on for too long, if I tire you with what I have to say, please interrupt me. I will not take offence. Throughout my life I have always said that all that matters is truth and truth is defended with truth. What I can say here is that my Defence, from my point of view, gathered a fair amount of evidence with which they attempted to prove my innocence. By chance today, on the 15th of May, it's been 59 months since I first came here, 59 months since I have been separated from my dear Mila and my dear family. But I won't tire you with this. For over 30 years I worked in a school. I taught young girls and boys. I taught them difficult subjects. I taught them mathematics and physics. And I always told them that there was nothing difficult about mathematics and physics. There are only things that one knows and things that one doesn't know. In the course of my professional experience, I attempted to convey knowledge as best I could and as successfully as I could to young people so that they might succeed as much as possible in life. And it was a great honour, and it was a matter of great satisfaction to me when I found out that these young people had reached a high level of education than I myself had. I treated my pupils in a correct manner. I always tried to be a second parent to them, and this humane attitude is something I learned from my parents. I learnt to love these children from them. And this attitude, this relationship with the pupils, and as I said, I worked with them for 30 years, also entailed a good relationship with parents and with other citizens. It was also transferred to these people. I have to admit that at all times there were various nationalities who were represented among the pupils and among the parents. I was never interested in the nationality of the children and of the parents. I was interested in the nature of the pupil and whether the pupil achieved good results and in whether the pupil could succeed in even more, because a good teacher is someone who attempts to transfer all his or her possibilities to the pupils. What happened is something that I could never have imagined at the age that I have now reached, this tragic war broke out, this fratricide broke out because before the war everyone lived together, everyone got on well. But then this dispute was suddenly -- suddenly broke out. Something happened that I wouldn't want to tire you with. My house burnt down in that war. You have heard that I have two sons who are seriously handicapped. I was burnt. I spent time in a hotel. I was then removed from the municipality and given a flat to rent. This is where I lived. That was not my only misfortune. There are other such people, Serbs, Muslims, and Croats, and members of other nationalities and a number of other people. I won't list them all and I won't waste your precious time. Other things happened too. I come from a peasant family that lived in a mountainous region where my late parents had nine children. Because of various circumstances in which they lived, because of the mountainous area, only four of them survived the Second World War. My father died in 1965. My mother died in 1967. In 1995, one of my brothers died. I came here in 1998. My sister died. And in February of this year, my other brother died. So out of the nine children, I'm the only one who is still alive, and this is where I am, before this Trial Chamber now. Naturally, this has all exerted an influence on me and has influenced my health. So in 2000, I had to undergo an operation here in the Detention Unit. My liver was operated on. I have recently had problems with the veins in my legs. My digestive system is causing me problems. I have -- my sight is not as good as it could be. I have problems with regards to my sight, and I've asked for my glasses to be changed for the fourth time because my sight is deteriorating. I have mentioned all these facts because the things I have been through, the things I have experienced show that even today, given all those conditions, all the misfortunes I have been through, in spite of all these misfortunes, there is not a shred of evil in me. I have -- I feel no hatred to any man of goodwill regardless of the nationality of that person or the social status of that person. I am certain that this Appeals Chamber will reach a fair decision, a just decision, and if possible, God willing, I hope that I will receive this decision in a better mood than the mood I am in at the moment, today. I would like to thank you, and I apologise. I didn't want to discuss the proceedings because the hearing has taken two days, and to me it seemed -- from my point of view it seemed to be quite professional and quite -- quite elaborate. That is why I didn't want to discuss the hearing. But I want to tell you that I bear no ill feelings towards anyone, especially since none of my brothers have lived beyond the age of 60, and within a month and a bit I'll be 63, and I probably won't live much longer than they did. Thank you, and I apologise again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may be seated at your place again.

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our hearing is now concluded. I would like to thank Defence counsel and the Prosecution for the proper attitude that they had all through these discussions and also thank our interpreters, faithful always, always at their posts, and having said this, I adjourn the hearing.
